poorer disk throughput and poorer disk space utilization
es_H2ApbCNICGlOJhWC.e:
**Key idea:** block size trades I/O efficiency against internal fragmentation.

**Throughput improves.** Disk access time is dominated by seek time and rotational latency, which are paid *per block access*. With larger blocks a file occupies fewer blocks, so reading it needs fewer accesses (and fewer pointer/index lookups); each access transfers more data for the same positioning overhead. Hence more bytes per second → **better throughput**.

**Space utilization worsens.** Space is allocated in whole blocks, so the last block of each file is on average about half empty. This internal fragmentation (≈ half a block per file) grows with the block size; with many small files, a large block wastes most of each block. Hence **poorer disk-space utilization**.

Example: a 1 KB file in a 64 KB-block file system wastes 63 KB, but a 64 MB file is read in 1024 accesses instead of 16384 with 4 KB blocks.

So (B), (C) and (D) all get at least one of the two effects backwards.

**Answer: (A)**

es_X1ztUCTV91yMUzlI.q:
Disk requests come to disk driver for cylinders \(10,22,20,2,40,6\) and \(38,\) in that order at a time when the disk drive is reading from cylinder \(20.\) The seek time is \(6msec\) per cylinder. Compute the total seek time if the disk arm scheduling algorithm is
(a) First come first served
(b) Closest cylinder next.
es_X1ztUCTV91yMUzlI.e:
**Key idea:** total seek time = (total cylinders travelled) × 6 ms. The head starts at cylinder 20.

**(a) First come first served**, which serves the requests in arrival order $10, 22, 20, 2, 40, 6, 38$:

| Move | Distance |
|---|---|
| 20 → 10 | 10 |
| 10 → 22 | 12 |
| 22 → 20 | 2 |
| 20 → 2 | 18 |
| 2 → 40 | 38 |
| 40 → 6 | 34 |
| 6 → 38 | 32 |
| **Total** | **146** |

Seek time $= 146 \times 6 = 876$ ms.

**(b) Closest cylinder next (SSTF)**, which always serves the nearest pending request:

| Head at | Nearest request | Distance |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 20 | 0 |
| 20 | 22 | 2 |
| 22 | 10 (12 away; 38 is 16 away) | 12 |
| 10 | 6 | 4 |
| 6 | 2 | 4 |
| 2 | 38 | 36 |
| 38 | 40 | 2 |
| **Total** | | **60** |

Seek time $= 60 \times 6 = 360$ ms.

**Answer:** (a) 876 ms; (b) 360 ms

es_FXoYCwk0vretKVfx.q:
State whether the following statements are TRUE or FALSE with reason.
The Link-load-and-go loading scheme requires less storage space than the Link-and-go loading scheme.
es_FXoYCwk0vretKVfx.e:
**Key idea:** what occupies memory while the program actually runs.

- **Link-and-go** (a linking loader): linking and loading happen in one step, directly in memory, immediately before execution. The **linker/loader program must be resident in memory together with the user program**, along with its symbol tables and the unlinked object modules it is processing.
- **Link-load-and-go** (linkage editor plus a separate simple loader): a linkage editor first produces a complete, already-linked load module. Later, a small relocating loader brings that module into memory and execution begins. At run time, **only the small loader (or nothing) and the linked program** are in memory. The large linker is not.

Because the linking program and its tables are not kept in memory beside the executing program, the link-load-and-go scheme needs less main-memory space. The price is the extra step of producing and storing the load module.

So the statement is **TRUE**.

**Answer: True**
es_FXoYCwk0vretKVfx.note: ExamSIDE lists False. In link-load-and-go the linker is not resident beside the running program, so it needs less memory. Loader schemes are outside the current GATE syllabus.

es_hrfk6oHxJZ5wtC7b.q: In a two-level virtual memory, the memory access time for main memory, \(t_M={10}^{-8}\sec\) and the memory access time for the secondary memory, \(t_S={10}^{-3}\sec .\) What must be the hit ratio, \(H\) such that the access efficiency is within \(80\) percent of its maximum value?
es_hrfk6oHxJZ5wtC7b.e:
**Key idea:** access efficiency is $e = t_M / t_{avg}$. Its maximum value of 1 is reached when every access hits in main memory, so "within 80% of the maximum" means $e \ge 0.8$.

The average access time is

$$t_{avg} = H\,t_M + (1-H)\,t_S.$$

The requirement is

$$\frac{t_M}{t_{avg}} \ge 0.8 \;\Rightarrow\; t_{avg} \le 1.25\,t_M = 1.25\times10^{-8}\text{ s}.$$

Substituting $t_M = 10^{-8}$ s and $t_S = 10^{-3}$ s:

$$H\cdot10^{-8} + (1-H)\cdot10^{-3} \le 1.25\times10^{-8}$$

$$\Rightarrow\;(1-H)\left(10^{-3}-10^{-8}\right) \le 0.25\times10^{-8}$$

$$\Rightarrow\; 1-H \le \frac{2.5\times10^{-9}}{0.99999\times10^{-3}} \approx 2.5\times10^{-6}.$$

So $H \ge 0.9999975$, i.e. about $99.99975\%$. The model $t_{avg} = t_M + (1-H)t_S$ gives the same bound to this precision.

Because $t_S / t_M = 10^5$, even one miss in 400,000 accesses costs 25% of the efficiency. For comparison, $H = 0.9999$ gives $t_{avg} \approx 1.1\times10^{-7}$ s, an efficiency of only about 9%.

**Answer: $H \ge 0.9999975$ (≈ 99.9998%)**
es_hrfk6oHxJZ5wtC7b.note: The commonly quoted "99.99%" is too loose: H = 0.9999 gives only about 9% efficiency. Requiring t_M / t_avg ≥ 0.8 gives H ≥ 0.9999975.

es_FmEuHgO6ZFcwrv10.q: State whether the following statement are TRUE or FALSE with reason. The data transfer between memory and \(\mathrm{I}/O\) devices using programmed \(\mathrm{I}/O\) is fasterthan interrrupt-driven \(\mathrm{I}/O\).
es_FmEuHgO6ZFcwrv10.e:
**Key idea:** in both schemes the **CPU itself moves every word** between memory and the device. The two schemes differ only in how the CPU learns that the device is ready.

- **Programmed I/O:** the CPU sits in a loop, repeatedly reading the device's status register until it is ready, and then transfers the word. All the time the device is busy is wasted in polling. The CPU can do nothing else, and with several devices it must poll them in turn, which delays service.
- **Interrupt-driven I/O:** the CPU issues the command and goes on with other work. The device raises an interrupt when it is ready, and the ISR transfers the data. The idle wait is overlapped with useful computation, so overall throughput of the system, and of I/O when several devices are active, is better.

The conventional answer is therefore that the statement is **FALSE**: programmed I/O is not the faster or more efficient way to transfer data, because the CPU wastes its time busy-waiting. Interrupt-driven I/O removes that waste, and DMA improves further on interrupt-driven I/O for bulk transfers.

(Strictly, for a *single* word on an otherwise idle CPU, a tight polling loop avoids the interrupt-entry and exit overhead and can react slightly sooner. The statement is judged at the level of overall transfer efficiency.)

**Answer: False**
es_FmEuHgO6ZFcwrv10.note: The conventional answer is False because programmed I/O wastes CPU time busy-waiting. Note that for a single word on an idle CPU, a tight polling loop avoids the interrupt overhead, so the wording is loose.

es_COvhSoTdYU0y44Gr.q:
A certain moving arm disk-storage device has the following specifications:
Number of tracks per surface \(=404\)
Track storage capacity \(=130030\) bytes
Disk speed \(=3600\) rpm
Average seek time \(=30\) m secs.
Estimate the average latency, the disk storage capacity, and the data transfer rate.
es_COvhSoTdYU0y44Gr.e:
**Key idea:**
- Rotational latency is on average half a revolution.
- Transfer rate is one track's worth of data per revolution.
- Capacity is tracks × track capacity, per recording surface.

The original paper gives **404** tracks per surface; the 4004 in the text is a typo.

**Rotation:**

$$3600 \text{ rpm} = 60 \text{ rev/s} \;\Rightarrow\; T_{rev} = \tfrac{1}{60}\text{ s} = 16.67\text{ ms}.$$

**Average latency:**

$$\tfrac{1}{2}\,T_{rev} = 8.33\text{ ms}.$$

**Storage capacity (per surface):**

$$404 \times 130030 = 52{,}532{,}120 \text{ bytes} \approx 52.5\text{ MB}.$$

The number of surfaces is not given. For $s$ surfaces, multiply by $s$.

**Data transfer rate:**

$$130030 \text{ bytes/rev} \times 60 \text{ rev/s} = 7{,}801{,}800 \text{ bytes/s} \approx 7.8\text{ MB/s}.$$

The average seek time of 30 ms is not needed for these three quantities. It would matter for the total average access time, which is $30 + 8.33 \approx 38.3$ ms plus the transfer time.

**Answer:** latency ≈ 8.33 ms; capacity ≈ 52.5 MB per surface; transfer rate ≈ 7.8 MB/s

es_ClBXSLSBRHMU01yG.q: Semaphore operations are atomic because they are implemented within the OS __________.
es_ClBXSLSBRHMU01yG.e:
**Key idea:** `wait` (P) and `signal` (V) each do a test-and-update on the semaphore value, and possibly block or wake a process. If two processes interleave inside these operations, updates can be lost. The operations must therefore be **indivisible**.

The OS guarantees this by implementing them as **system calls in the kernel**.
- On a uniprocessor, the kernel code can disable interrupts during the short critical update, so no context switch can occur in the middle.
- On a multiprocessor, the kernel additionally protects the semaphore with a hardware atomic instruction such as test-and-set or compare-and-swap (a spinlock).

The kernel also manages the waiting queue. It can block the caller and later wake it, which user code cannot do safely by itself.

**Answer: kernel**

es_aNMRUsM97EZk7WLn.q: Under paged memory management scheme simple lock and key memory protection arrangement may still be required if the  \(........\) processors do not have address mapping hardware.
es_aNMRUsM97EZk7WLn.e:
**Key idea:** paging protects memory because every CPU-generated address passes through the page table. A process cannot even name a frame that is not mapped for it.

Not every agent that touches memory goes through that mapping. **I/O processors**, such as DMA controllers and I/O channels, often work directly with **physical addresses** and have no address-translation hardware of their own. A faulty or misprogrammed I/O transfer could then overwrite any frame, including frames that belong to other processes or to the OS.

To guard against this, a simple **lock-and-key** scheme can still be used:
- Each memory block carries a protection key (the lock).
- Each I/O transfer is tagged with a key.
- An access is allowed only when the two match.

This is why paged systems such as the IBM 370 kept storage keys even with paging.

**Answer: Input-output (I/O)**

es_biBPV8ITk8BevBor.q:
Match the pairs in the following Question.

List I

(A) Critical region
(B) Wait/Signal
(C) Working set
(D) Deadlock

List II

(p) Hoare's monitor
(q) Mutual exclusion
(r) Principle of locality
(s) Circular wait
es_biBPV8ITk8BevBor.e:
Match each concept with the idea it is built on or the problem it addresses:

- **(A) Critical region → (q) Mutual exclusion.** A critical region is a block of code that only one process may execute at a time, so mutual exclusion is exactly its purpose.
- **(B) Wait/Signal → (p) Hoare's monitor.** In Hoare's monitors, processes synchronise on condition variables using the `wait` and `signal` operations.
- **(C) Working set → (r) Principle of locality.** The working set model assumes a process uses a small, slowly changing set of pages over a window of time. That assumption is the principle of locality.
- **(D) Deadlock → (s) Circular wait.** Circular wait is one of the four necessary (Coffman) conditions for deadlock, and the characteristic one.

**Answer: A-q, B-p, C-r, D-s**

es_SJV9fjw3eqBX5KDh.q: State whether the following statements are TRUE or FALSE with reason. Transferring data in blocks from the main memory to the cache memory enables an interleaved main memory unit to operate unit at its maximum speed.
es_SJV9fjw3eqBX5KDh.e:
**Key idea:** in a low-order interleaved memory, *consecutive* addresses fall in *different* memory modules, and these modules can operate concurrently.

A cache miss brings in a whole **block**, a run of consecutive words. With $k$-way low-order interleaving, the words of that block lie in $k$ different modules. The memory controller can therefore:
- start an access in every module, one after the other, a few cycles apart;
- have all $k$ module cycles overlap; and
- receive one word per bus cycle instead of one word per full memory cycle.

The full parallelism of the interleaved organisation is used only when many consecutive words are requested together. Block transfer from main memory to cache creates exactly that access pattern.

If words were requested one at a time, each request would occupy one module for a full cycle while the others sat idle, and interleaving would gain nothing. Hence block transfer is what lets an interleaved memory run at its **maximum speed** (bandwidth).

**Answer: True**
es_SJV9fjw3eqBX5KDh.note: ExamSIDE lists False, but block transfers request consecutive words that sit in different interleaved modules, so all modules work in parallel, which is how interleaving reaches its peak bandwidth.

es_xwJHGDH5WoxgUNj9.q: Assume that there are \(3\) page frames which are initially empty. If the page reference string is \(1,2,3,4,2,1,5,3,2,4,6,\) the number of page faults using the optimal replacement policy is______________.
es_xwJHGDH5WoxgUNj9.e:
**Optimal replacement** evicts the resident page whose next use is farthest in the future, or that is never used again.

The reference string is $1,2,3,4,2,1,5,3,2,4,6$, with 3 frames.

| Ref | Frames after | Result | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | F | |
| 2 | 1 2 | F | |
| 3 | 1 2 3 | F | |
| 4 | 1 2 4 | F | next uses: 2 → pos 5, 1 → pos 6, 3 → pos 8; evict **3** |
| 2 | 1 2 4 | H | |
| 1 | 1 2 4 | H | |
| 5 | 5 2 4 | F | 1 is never used again; evict **1** |
| 3 | 3 2 4 | F | 5 is never used again; evict **5** |
| 2 | 3 2 4 | H | |
| 4 | 3 2 4 | H | |
| 6 | 6 2 4 (any) | F | none of 3, 2, 4 is used again |

Faults occur at references 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 3 and 6, for a total of **7**.

**Answer: 7**

es_ZuvvYYVoMO88KtpQ.q: Suppose a disk has 201 cylinders, numbered from 0 to 200. At some time the disk arm is at cylinder 100, and there is a queue of disk access requests for cylinders 30, 85, 90, 100, 105, 110, 135 and 145. If Shortest-Seek Time First (SSTF) is being used for scheduling the disk access, the request for cylinder 90 is serviced after servicing ____________ number of requests.
es_ZuvvYYVoMO88KtpQ.e:
SSTF always serves the pending request nearest to the current arm position, in either direction.

Arm at 100. Queue: 30, 85, 90, 100, 105, 110, 135, 145.

1. **100.** Distance 0, since the arm is already there. Serviced first.
2. From 100: 105 is 5 away, while 90 is 10 away. Serve **105**.
3. From 105: 110 is 5 away, while 90 is 15 away. Serve **110**.
4. From 110: 90 is 20 away, while 135 is 25 away. Serve **90**.

The requests serviced before 90 are 100, 105 and 110, i.e., **3** requests.

(Afterwards SSTF continues 85, 30, 135, 145.)

**Answer: 3**

es_c8vPsbBIZvcaB4m8.q:
An operating system uses the Banker’s algorithm for deadlock avoidance when managing the allocation of three resource types X, Y, and Z to three processes P0, P1, and P2. The table given below presents the current system state. Here, the Allocation matrix shows the current number of resources of each type allocated to each process and the Max matrix shows the maximum number of resources of each type required by each process during its execution. There are 3 units of type X, 2 units of type Y and 2 units of type Z still available. The system is currently in a safe state. Consider the following independent requests for additional resources in the current state:

REQ1: P0 requests 0 units of X, 0 units of Y and 2 units of Z
REQ2: P1 requests 2 units of X, 0 units of Y and 0 units of Z

Which one of the following is TRUE?
o: Both REQ1 and REQ2 can be permitted.
Neither REQ1 nor REQ2 can be permitted
es_c8vPsbBIZvcaB4m8.e:
**Need = Max − Allocation**, with Available $=(3,2,2)$:

| | Allocation | Max | Need |
|---|---|---|---|
| P0 | (0,0,1) | (8,4,3) | (8,4,2) |
| P1 | (3,2,0) | (6,2,0) | (3,0,0) |
| P2 | (2,1,1) | (3,3,3) | (1,2,2) |

To check a request, pretend to grant it and run the safety algorithm.

**REQ1: P0 asks for (0,0,2).** The request is within P0's need and within Available. After granting:
- Available $=(3,2,0)$ and Need(P0) $=(8,4,0)$.
- Safety check: P1's need $(3,0,0)\le(3,2,0)$, so P1 can finish. Work becomes $(3,2,0)+(3,2,0)=(6,4,0)$.
- P2 needs 2 units of Z but 0 are available. P0 needs 8 units of X but only 6 are available. Neither can finish.

The resulting state is **unsafe**, so REQ1 is denied.

**REQ2: P1 asks for (2,0,0).** The request is within P1's need $(3,0,0)$ and within Available. After granting:
- Available $=(1,2,2)$, Alloc(P1) $=(5,2,0)$, Need(P1) $=(1,0,0)$.
- P1 finishes: Work $=(1,2,2)+(5,2,0)=(6,4,2)$.
- P2's need $(1,2,2)\le(6,4,2)$, so P2 finishes: Work $=(8,5,3)$.
- P0's need $(8,4,2)\le(8,5,3)$, so P0 finishes.

The safe sequence is $\langle P1, P2, P0\rangle$, so REQ2 can be granted.

Only REQ2 can be permitted.

**Answer: (B)**

es_e1lkaSXIi2x6L5r9.q: Consider a system with \(3\) processes that share \(4\) instances of the same resource type. Each process can request a maximum of \(K\) instances. Resource instances can be requested and released only one at a time. The largest value of \(K\) that will always avoid deadlock is ____.
es_e1lkaSXIi2x6L5r9.e:
Worst case: every process holds $K - 1$ instances and waits for one more. Deadlock is impossible if even then one instance is still free, so that some process can finish and release its instances:
$$3(K-1) + 1 \le 4 \;\Rightarrow\; 3K \le 6 \;\Rightarrow\; K \le 2.$$

- $K = 2$: at most 3 instances are held while all three wait, so 1 is free and someone completes. Deadlock-free.
- $K = 3$: the processes could hold 2, 1, 1 (all 4 instances) and each wait for more, so deadlock is possible.

**Answer: 2**

es_Qq9xGKp3mFwUl3oCpt1da9i2ynkcvfg2bo.q:
Consider the following set of processes, assumed to have arrived at time 0. Consider the CPU scheduling algorithms Shortest Job First (SJF) and Round Robin (RR). For RR, assume that the processes are scheduled in the order P1, P2, P3, P4.
If the time quantum for RR is 4 ms, then the absolute value of the difference between the average turnaround times (in ms) of SJF and RR (round off to 2 decimal places) is _____.
es_Qq9xGKp3mFwUl3oCpt1da9i2ynkcvfg2bo.e:
**Key idea:** all four processes arrive at time 0, so turnaround time equals completion time. The bursts are P1 = 8, P2 = 7, P3 = 2, P4 = 4.

**SJF** (shortest burst first): P3, P4, P2, P1.

| Interval | 0–2 | 2–6 | 6–13 | 13–21 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Process | P3 | P4 | P2 | P1 |

Completion times: P3 = 2, P4 = 6, P2 = 13, P1 = 21.

$$\text{Avg TAT}_{SJF} = \frac{2+6+13+21}{4} = \frac{42}{4} = 10.5$$

**RR** (quantum 4, order P1, P2, P3, P4)

| Interval | Process | Left after |
|---|---|---|
| 0–4 | P1 | 4 |
| 4–8 | P2 | 3 |
| 8–10 | P3 | done at 10 |
| 10–14 | P4 | done at 14 |
| 14–18 | P1 | done at 18 |
| 18–21 | P2 | done at 21 |

$$\text{Avg TAT}_{RR} = \frac{18+21+10+14}{4} = \frac{63}{4} = 15.75$$

**Difference:** $|10.5 - 15.75| = 5.25$

**Answer: 5.25**

es_6iYYSZS26XolR1pV.q: Match the pairs in the following question by writing the corresponding letters only.
es_6iYYSZS26XolR1pV.e:
List I: (A) Buddy system, (B) Interpretation, (C) Pointer type, (D) Virtual memory.
List II: (P) Run-time type specification, (Q) Segmentation, (R) Memory allocation, (S) Garbage collection.

- **Buddy system → Memory allocation (R).** The buddy system allocates memory by splitting free blocks into power-of-two halves ("buddies") and merging them back when freed.
- **Interpretation → Run-time type specification (P).** An interpreter executes the program directly, without a separate compile step, so it can determine and check types at run time (dynamic typing).
- **Pointer type → Garbage collection (S).** With pointers, heap objects can become unreachable. Reclaiming those objects is the job of garbage collection.
- **Virtual memory → Segmentation (Q).** Segmentation, like paging, is one way to implement virtual memory.

**Answer: A-R, B-P, C-S, D-Q**

es_zGFKWzz2N5qODOEH.q: The total size of address space in a virtual memory systems is limited by
es_zGFKWzz2N5qODOEH.e:
**Key idea:** an *address space* is the set of addresses a program can generate. With an $n$-bit address it holds exactly $2^n$ locations, however much physical storage exists.

- **(A) Length of MAR.** The memory address register holds the address the processor sends out, so its width $n$ fixes the address space at $2^n$. This is the limit on the *size of the address space*.
- **(B) Available secondary storage.** This limits how much of the virtual space can actually be *backed* by pages on disk, i.e. how much virtual memory is usable. It does not change how many addresses exist.
- **(C) Available main memory.** Removing this limit is the whole purpose of virtual memory, so it is clearly wrong.
- **(D) All of the above.** Wrong, because (C) is wrong.

**Answer: (A)**
es_zGFKWzz2N5qODOEH.note: ExamSIDE lists (B), but the size of the address space is fixed by the address width (MAR length); secondary storage limits how much of that space can actually be backed. The original 1991 question allowed more than one choice, and some sources accept (A) and (B) together.

es_6GFzAjHgXljmRc80.q: A ''link editor'' is a program that:
o: Matches the parameters of the macro definition with locations of the parameters of the macro call.
Matches external names of one program with their location in other programs.
Matches the parameters of subroutine definition with the location of parameters of subroutine call.
Acts as a link between compiler and user program.
es_6GFzAjHgXljmRc80.e:
A **link editor (linker)** combines separately compiled or assembled object modules into one executable. Its central job is **symbol resolution**.

A module may refer to *external* names: functions or variables defined in some other module. The compiler cannot know where these will end up, so it leaves them as unresolved references. The linker matches each external name with its definition in another module, fills in that address, and relocates addresses as the modules are placed together. In other words, it matches the external names of one program with their locations in other programs.

Why the other options fail:

- **(A)** Binding a macro's formal parameters to the actual arguments of a macro call is done by a **macro processor**.
- **(C)** Matching subroutine parameters with the arguments at a call is handled by the calling sequence that the compiler generates and that runs at run time. The linker does not do it.
- **(D)** The linker does not act as a link between the compiler and the user program. It runs after compilation, on the object code.

**Answer: (B)**

es_6ndQNl0AoBfhKK62.q: Consider a computer system with ten physical page frames. The system is provided with an access sequence \((a_1,a_2,....,a_{20},a_1,a_2,...,a_{20}),\) where each \(a_i\) is a distinct virtual page number. The difference in the number of page faults between the last-in-first-out page replacement policy and the optimal page replacement policy is _____________
es_6ndQNl0AoBfhKK62.e:
10 frames, reference string $a_1, \dots, a_{20}, a_1, \dots, a_{20}$.

**First pass (both policies):** all 20 references are first-time references, so 20 compulsory faults.

**LIFO** (evict the page brought in most recently):
- $a_1$ to $a_{10}$ fill the frames. Each of $a_{11}$ to $a_{20}$ evicts the previous newcomer, so after pass 1 the frames hold $a_1$ to $a_9$ and $a_{20}$.
- Pass 2: $a_1$ to $a_9$ hit. $a_{10}$ faults (evicting $a_{20}$), then each of $a_{11}$ to $a_{20}$ faults, evicting the previous newcomer. That is 11 faults.
- Total $= 20 + 11 = 31$.

**Optimal** (evict the page whose next use is farthest away):
- In pass 1, for each of $a_{11}$ to $a_{20}$ the resident page used farthest in the future is the latest newcomer, so after pass 1 the frames again hold $a_1$ to $a_9$ and $a_{20}$.
- Pass 2: $a_1$ to $a_9$ hit. For $a_{10}$ to $a_{19}$, evict pages that are never used again and keep $a_{20}$: 10 faults. Then $a_{20}$ hits.
- Total $= 20 + 10 = 30$. No policy can do better, because a page loaded during pass 2 is never reused, so at most 10 hits are possible in pass 2.

Difference $= 31 - 30 = 1$.

**Answer: 1**

es_R1MLRaf7sl0MeJ8m.q:
The address sequence generated by tracing a particular program executing in a pure demand paging system with \(100\) records per page with \(1\) free main memory frame is recorded as follows. What is the number of page faults?

\(0100,0200,0430,0499,0510,0530,0560,0120,0220,0240,0260,0320,0370\)
es_R1MLRaf7sl0MeJ8m.e:
**Page numbers:** with 100 records per page, page number $=\lfloor \text{address}/100 \rfloor$.

| Address | 0100 | 0200 | 0430 | 0499 | 0510 | 0530 | 0560 | 0120 | 0220 | 0240 | 0260 | 0320 | 0370 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Page | 1 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 3 |

With only **one** frame and pure demand paging (memory starts empty), a reference causes a fault exactly when its page differs from the page referenced just before it. The very first reference also faults.

Collapsing consecutive repeats gives the pages that fault: 1, 2, 4, 5, 1, 2, 3. That is **7 page faults**.

**Answer: (C)**

es_VR0abz4kw2DsQHQ4.q: In a virtual memory system the address space specified by the address lines of the \(CPU\) must be __________ than the physical memory size and _______ than the secondary storage size.
es_VR0abz4kw2DsQHQ4.e:
**Key idea:** virtual memory lets a program use an address space bigger than the installed RAM. Pages that are not in RAM are kept on secondary storage (the swap area or backing store).

- The virtual address space, set by the CPU's address lines, should be **larger than physical memory**. If it were not, all of it would fit in RAM and there would be no need for virtual memory.
- It must be **smaller than secondary storage** (at most equal to it), because every virtual page needs a home on the backing store whenever it is not in RAM.

**Example:** 32-bit virtual addresses give a 4 GB virtual space, with perhaps 1 GB of RAM and a disk far larger than 4 GB.

**Answer: (C)**

es_4hiPuR4H5HO33xXz.q:
A computer installation has 1000K of main memory. The jobs arrive and finish in the following sequence.
Job 1 requiring 200k arrives
Job 2 requiring 350k arrives
Job 3 requiring 300k arrives
Job 1 finishes
Job 4 requiring 120k arrives
Job 5 requiring 150k arrives
Job 6 requiring 80k arrives

(a) Draw the memory allocation table using Best Fit and First fit algorithm.
(b) Which algorithm performs better for this sequence?
es_4hiPuR4H5HO33xXz.e:
**Common start** (memory 0–1000K):
- J1 takes 0–200, J2 takes 200–550, J3 takes 550–850. The hole 850–1000 (150K) is free.
- J1 finishes, so the holes are **0–200 (200K)** and **850–1000 (150K)**.

**First fit** – use the first hole that is large enough:

| Job | Hole chosen | Placed at | Holes after |
|---|---|---|---|
| J4 (120K) | 0–200 | 0–120 | 120–200 (80K), 850–1000 (150K) |
| J5 (150K) | 850–1000 (the 80K hole is too small) | 850–1000 | 120–200 (80K) |
| J6 (80K) | 120–200 | 120–200 | none |

All jobs are placed, and memory is 100% used.

**Best fit** – use the smallest hole that is large enough:

| Job | Hole chosen | Placed at | Holes after |
|---|---|---|---|
| J4 (120K) | 850–1000 (150K is smaller than 200K) | 850–970 | 0–200 (200K), 970–1000 (30K) |
| J5 (150K) | 0–200 | 0–150 | 150–200 (50K), 970–1000 (30K) |
| J6 (80K) | no hole ≥ 80K | **cannot be allocated** | 50K, 30K |

$80$K is free in total, but it is split into $50$K and $30$K holes, so J6 must wait. This is external fragmentation.

**(b)** For this sequence **first fit performs better**: it accommodates every job, while best fit leaves J6 waiting.

**Answer: First fit is better (all jobs allocated); best fit fails to allocate Job 6**

es_U4eMBPHCrk49Sfki.q: The capacity of a memory unit is defined by the number of words multiplied by the number of bits/word. How many separate address and data lines are needed for a memory of \(4K\;\; \times\;\; 16?\)
es_U4eMBPHCrk49Sfki.e:
A memory of size (number of words) × (bits per word) needs

- $\log_2(\text{number of words})$ address lines, enough to select any one word, and
- (bits per word) data lines, enough to transfer one whole word at a time.

For $4K \times 16$:

- Number of words $= 4 \times 2^{10} = 2^{12}$, so it needs **12 address lines**.
- Word size $= 16$ bits, so it needs **16 data lines**.

**Answer: (C)**

es_kWTdHFeNVLTTt2L3.q: Which of the following scheduling algorithms is non-preemptive?
es_kWTdHFeNVLTTt2L3.e:
**Key idea:** a scheduler is *non-preemptive* if, once a process gets the CPU, it keeps it until it terminates or blocks voluntarily (e.g. for I/O); the OS never forcibly takes the CPU away.

- **FIFO / FCFS** — the process at the head of the ready queue runs until it finishes or blocks; a newly arrived process simply joins the tail. **Non-preemptive.**
- **Round Robin** — a timer interrupt takes the CPU away when the time quantum expires → preemptive by design.
- **Multilevel queue scheduling** — queues have fixed priorities; a process arriving in a higher-priority queue preempts a running lower-priority process (and queues often use RR internally) → preemptive.
- **Multilevel feedback queue** — processes are preempted at quantum expiry and moved between queues; higher-queue arrivals preempt → preemptive.

**Answer: (B)**

es_kGl9WsRHDif5OI55.q:
Which combination of the following features will suffice to characterize an \(OS\) as a multi-programmed \(OS?\)
\((a).\) More than one program may be loaded into main memory at the same time for execution.
\((b).\) If a program waits for certain events such as \(I/O\), another program is immediately scheduled for execution.
\((c).\) If the execution of a program terminates, another program is immediately scheduled for execution.
es_kGl9WsRHDif5OI55.e:
**Key idea:** the purpose of multiprogramming is to keep the CPU busy by overlapping one program's I/O with another program's computation. That requires two things:

- **(a)** Several programs resident in main memory at the same time — otherwise there is nothing ready to switch to without a slow load from disk.
- **(b)** When the running program waits for an event such as I/O, the CPU is **immediately** given to another ready program.

Together these define a multiprogrammed OS, so (a) and (b) suffice.

- **(a) alone** is not enough: if programs merely sit in memory but the CPU idles while the current one waits for I/O, there is no multiprogramming benefit.
- **(c)** — starting the next program when the current one terminates — happens in an ordinary *uniprogrammed* batch system too, so it does not characterise multiprogramming and is not needed in the combination.

**Answer: (B)**

es_v2tL56JsWxpX2B7j.e:
A deadlock needs a **circular wait**. Each process holds its first resource while it waits for its second:
- even $P_i$: holds $R_i$, wants $R_{i+2}$ (increasing order);
- odd $P_j$: holds $R_{n-j}$, wants $R_{n-j-2}$ (decreasing order).

Each step in a wait-for chain moves the resource index by $\pm 2$, and the resources in a cycle must be distinct. So the only possible cycle is between one even and one odd process that request the same two resources in opposite order:
$$R_i = R_{n-j-2},\quad R_{i+2} = R_{n-j} \;\Longrightarrow\; i + j = n-2.$$
Here $i$ is even and $j$ is odd, so $i+j$ is odd. That means $n$ must be **odd**. Both processes must also exist ($i, j \le k-1$) and make two requests ($i+2<n$, $j+2<n$).

Checking the options:
- **(A)** $n=40$ and **(C)** $n=20$ are even, so no deadlock is possible.
- **(D)** $n=41$ needs $i+j=39$, but with $k=19$ the largest even + odd pair is $18+17=35$. No deadlock.
- **(B)** $n=21$, $k=12$ needs $i+j=19$, and $i=8, j=11$ works. $P_8$ requests $R_8$ then $R_{10}$, while $P_{11}$ requests $R_{10}$ then $R_8$. If $P_8$ holds $R_8$ and $P_{11}$ holds $R_{10}$, each waits forever for the other. ($i=10, j=9$ deadlocks the same way on $R_{10}, R_{12}$.)

**Answer: (B)**

es_FIYOsRb7TTkgXsSi.q:
The details of an interrupt cycle are shown in Figure
Given that an interrupt input arrives every \(1\) \(msec,\) what is the percentage of the total time that the \(CPU\) devotes for the main program execution.
es_FIYOsRb7TTkgXsSi.e:
**Key idea:** each interrupt takes CPU time away from the main program for saving the CPU state, running the service routine and restoring the state. The main program's share is whatever is left of each interrupt period.

From the figure, per interrupt:
- Saving CPU state: $10\ \mu s$
- Interrupt service routine: $80\ \mu s$
- Restoring CPU state: $10\ \mu s$

Total overhead $= 10 + 80 + 10 = 100\ \mu s$.

The $10\ \mu s$ marked right after the interrupt arrives is the response delay, during which the CPU is still finishing main-program work. It coincides with the time before state saving starts, so it is not extra overhead.

An interrupt arrives every $1\text{ ms} = 1000\ \mu s$, so the main program gets
$$\frac{1000 - 100}{1000} \times 100\% = 90\%.$$

**Answer: 90%**

es_PJtLxMJnaOdO99kD.q:
Assume that the following jobs are to be executed on a single processor system.
Job Id CPU Burst Time
p 4
q 1
r 8
s 1
t 2

The jobs are assumed to have arrived at time \(0^+\) and in the order \(p,q,r,s,t.\) Calculate the departure time (completion time) for job \(p\) if scheduling is round robin with time slice\(1.\)
es_PJtLxMJnaOdO99kD.e:
**Setup:** round robin with quantum 1. All jobs arrive at $0^+$ in the order p, q, r, s, t, and a preempted job goes to the back of the ready queue.

| Time | Runs | After this slice |
|---|---|---|
| 0–1 | p | p has 3 left |
| 1–2 | q | q done at 2 |
| 2–3 | r | r has 7 left |
| 3–4 | s | s done at 4 |
| 4–5 | t | t has 1 left |
| 5–6 | p | p has 2 left |
| 6–7 | r | r has 6 left |
| 7–8 | t | t done at 8 |
| 8–9 | p | p has 1 left |
| 9–10 | r | r has 5 left |
| 10–11 | p | **p done at 11** |

Job p completes (departs) at time 11.

**Answer: (C)**

es_CUcGjMNXHrO6SDnb.q: A simple two-pass assembler does the following in the first pass:
o: It allocates space for the literals.
It computes the total length of the program
It builds the symbol table for the symbols and their values.
It generates code for all the load and store register instructions.
es_CUcGjMNXHrO6SDnb.e:
**Why two passes?** Forward references: a symbol may be used before it is defined. So the first pass only *collects information and assigns addresses*, and the second pass *generates code* using that information.

**Pass 1 work:**
- Maintains a location counter (LC) and assigns an address to every statement.
- **Builds the symbol table (C).** Each label gets the current LC value.
- **Handles literals (A).** Literals go into a literal table, and at `LTORG`/`END` the literal pool is given addresses, so space for the literals is allocated in pass 1.
- **Computes the total program length (B).** This is the final LC minus the start address. It is needed for the object-program header and by the loader.
- Processes directives that affect the LC, such as `START`, `ORG`, `DS`/`RESW` and `EQU`.

**Pass 2 work:** generates machine code for *all* instructions, including load/store, using the symbol and literal tables, and writes the object program. So (D) is a pass-2 activity. Pass 1 cannot generate correct code for instructions that refer to symbols defined later.

**Answer: (A), (B), (C)**
es_CUcGjMNXHrO6SDnb.note: ExamSIDE lists only (C), but pass 1 also assigns addresses to the literal pool and computes the program length; only code generation (D) waits for pass 2.

es_NpdF6raZtsIIsMIu.q: A part of the system software, which under all circumstances must reside in the main memory is:
es_NpdF6raZtsIIsMIu.e:
**Key idea:** the **loader** is the program that brings every other program into main memory and prepares it to run. This includes the editor, assembler, linker, compiler and user programs.

Each of those programs is needed only now and then. It can be loaded when it is needed and its memory reused afterwards. The loader is different, because it cannot load itself: if it were not already in memory, nothing could be brought into memory. So the loader (at least its resident part) must stay in main memory at all times. At power-on, a tiny bootstrap loader in ROM loads the operating system, including the loader, and from then on the loader loads everything else.

- **(A) Text editor, (B) assembler, (C) linker:** these are ordinary programs. The loader brings them in on demand, so they need not stay in memory.

**Answer: (D)**

es_Nl9ZFlhBWunAlgel.q: Which one of the following is FALSE?
o: User level threads are not scheduled by the kernel.
When a user level thread is blocked, all other threads of its process are blocked.
Context switching between user level threads is faster than context switching between kernel level threads.
Kernel level threads cannot share the code segment.
es_Nl9ZFlhBWunAlgel.e:
- **(A) True.** User-level threads are created and scheduled by a thread library in user space. The kernel sees only the process, or one kernel thread, and knows nothing about the individual user-level threads.
- **(B) True.** In the pure user-level (many-to-one) model, a blocking system call made by one thread blocks the single kernel entity behind the whole process, so all its threads stop.
- **(C) True.** Switching between user-level threads is just a library routine that saves and restores registers in user space. There is no mode switch and no kernel scheduler involved, so it is faster than a kernel-thread switch.
- **(D) False.** Threads of the same process, whether user-level or kernel-level, share the code segment, along with data, heap and open files. Each thread has a private copy only of its stack, registers and PC.

**Answer: (D)**

es_Rr10b0crfTmVgwYV.q:
Consider the following set of processes that need to be scheduled on a single \(CPU.\) All the times are given in milliseconds.
Process Name Arrival Time Execution Time
A 0 6
B 3 2
C 5 4
D 7 6
E 10 3

Using the \(shortest\) \(remaining\) \(time\) \(first\) scheduling algorithm, the average process turnaround time (in \(msec\)) is _______.
es_Rr10b0crfTmVgwYV.e:
SRTF runs the process with the least **remaining** time and re-decides whenever a process arrives or finishes.

- $t=0$: A runs (6).
- $t=3$: B arrives (2) while A has 3 left. B preempts A and runs $3$–$5$.
- $t=5$: B finishes. C arrives (4) while A has 3 left. A runs.
- $t=7$: D arrives (6) while A has 1 left. A continues and finishes at $8$.
- $t=8$: C (4) and D (6) are ready. C runs.
- $t=10$: E arrives (3) while C has 2 left. C continues and finishes at $12$.
- $t=12$: E (3) and D (6) are ready. E runs $12$–$15$, then D runs $15$–$21$.

Gantt chart: `A 0–3 | B 3–5 | A 5–8 | C 8–12 | E 12–15 | D 15–21`

| Process | Arrival | Completion | Turnaround |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | 8 | 8 |
| B | 3 | 5 | 2 |
| C | 5 | 12 | 7 |
| D | 7 | 21 | 14 |
| E | 10 | 15 | 5 |

Average turnaround time $=\dfrac{8+2+7+14+5}{5}=\dfrac{36}{5}=7.2$ ms.

**Answer: 7.2**

es_32TBxCrou4IJWZuD.q:
Consider a process executing on an operating system that uses demand paging. The average time for a memory access in the system is \(M\) units if the corresponding memory page is available in memory, and \(D\) units if the memory access causes a page fault. It has been experimentally measured that the average time taken for a memory access in the process is \(X\) units.

Which one of the following is the correct expression for the page fault rate experienced by the process?
es_32TBxCrou4IJWZuD.e:
Let $p$ be the page fault rate. The measured average access time is the weighted average of the two cases:
$$X = (1-p)\,M + p\,D = M + p\,(D - M).$$

Solving for $p$:
$$p = \frac{X - M}{D - M}.$$

Sanity check: if $X = M$ (no faults) then $p = 0$; if $X = D$ (every access faults) then $p = 1$. Option (C) is $1 - p$ (the hit rate), and (A) and (D) fail these boundary cases.

**Answer: (B)**

es_ZeuCjgQb6U2XTs3Q.e:
**Key idea — Peterson's algorithm:** process $i$ announces interest (`flag[i] = true`) and politely gives the turn away (`turn = j`). It must then wait **only while the other process is interested *and* it is the other's turn**:
$$P \;=\; (\text{flag}[j] = \text{true}) \wedge (\text{turn} = j).$$

**Why it works:** if both processes are trying, both flags are true, and `turn` holds whichever value was written *last*. Exactly one of them sees `turn` pointing to the other and waits, so they can never both be in the CS. If $j$ is not interested, `flag[j]` is false and $i$ enters immediately (progress).

**Why the other options fail:**
- **(A)** `flag[j] && turn == i`: $i$ sets `turn = j`, finds `flag[j]` false and enters. Then $j$ sets `turn = i`, its predicate `flag[i] && turn == j` is false, and it enters too — **both in the CS**.
- **(D)** `flag[i] && turn == i`: $i$ just set `turn = j`, so it usually passes at once; symmetrically $j$ passes too — mutual exclusion is violated.
- **(C)** `flag[i] && turn == j`: `flag[i]` is always true for $i$, so this reduces to "wait while turn = j". This forces strict alternation: a process trying alone waits forever (no progress), so it is not a correct critical-section solution.

**Answer: (B)**

es_hXKzCzewcbnnL5Ro.q: Which of the following statements is false?
o: Virtual memory implements the translation of a program’s address space into physical memory address space
Virtual memory allows each program to exceed the size of the primary memory
Virtual memory increases the degree of multiprogramming.
Virtual memory reduces the context switching overhead.
es_hXKzCzewcbnnL5Ro.e:
**Key idea:** virtual memory maps each process's logical address space onto physical memory, with secondary storage as backing store.

- **(A) True.** Translating a program's (virtual) addresses into physical addresses through page tables or the MMU is exactly what virtual memory does.
- **(B) True.** Only the working set needs to be resident, so a program can be larger than main memory.
- **(C) True.** Each process needs only part of its pages in memory, so more processes fit at once.
- **(D) False.** Virtual memory *adds* context-switch work. On every switch the OS must:
  - change the page-table base register,
  - flush the TLB (or tag its entries),
  - and absorb the extra TLB misses and page faults that follow when the new process restarts.

  It does not reduce context-switch overhead.

**Answer: (D)**
es_hXKzCzewcbnnL5Ro.note: ExamSIDE lists (A), but address translation is exactly what virtual memory does; the false statement is (D), because virtual memory adds context-switch work (page-table switch, TLB flush).

es_LVVIHI5IlkXW0Uzm.q: Consider a virtual memory system with \(FIFO\) page replacement policy. For an arbitrary page access pattern, increasing the number of page frames in main memory will
o: Always decrease the number of page faults.
Always increase the number of page faults.
Sometimes increase the number of page faults.
Never affect the number of page faults.
es_LVVIHI5IlkXW0Uzm.e:
**Key idea — Belady's anomaly:** FIFO is not a *stack algorithm*: the set of pages held with $n$ frames is not necessarily a subset of the set held with $n+1$ frames. Hence, for some reference strings, giving FIFO **more** frames produces **more** page faults.

Classic example: reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

- 3 frames → **9** page faults
- 4 frames → **10** page faults

For most reference strings more frames reduce (or do not change) the faults, but the anomaly shows this is not guaranteed. So the effect is: *sometimes* the number of page faults increases.

- (A) "Always decrease" — false (Belady's anomaly, and also sometimes there is no change).
- (B) "Always increase" — false; usually faults decrease.
- (D) "Never affect" — false.

**Answer: (C)**

es_k5C0VEcHFN6am84f.q:
The overlay tree for a program is as shown below:

What will be the size of the partition (in physical memory) required to load (and run) this program?
es_k5C0VEcHFN6am84f.e:
**Key idea:** with overlays, only the modules on **one root-to-leaf path** of the overlay tree are in memory at any time (siblings share the same memory area and overwrite each other). So the partition must be as large as the **heaviest root-to-leaf path**.

Sizes: Root = 2 KB; A = 4, B = 6, C = 8 KB; D = 6, E = 8 (children of A), F = 2 (child of B), G = 4 KB (child of C).

| Path | Size |
|---|---|
| Root–A–D | $2 + 4 + 6 = 12$ KB |
| Root–A–E | $2 + 4 + 8 = 14$ KB |
| Root–B–F | $2 + 6 + 2 = 10$ KB |
| Root–C–G | $2 + 8 + 4 = 14$ KB |

Maximum = **14 KB**, which is enough for every path; anything smaller (12, 10, 8 KB) cannot hold Root–A–E or Root–C–G.

**Answer: (B)**

es_tK3sjaJhet2ypch2.q: If an instruction takes \(\mathrm{I}\) microseconds and a page fault takes an additional \(j\) microseconds, the effective instruction time if on the average a page fault occurs every \(k\) instruction is:
es_tK3sjaJhet2ypch2.e:
**Key idea:** average the extra page-fault cost over the instructions that share it.

- Every instruction costs $i$ µs.
- On average one page fault occurs per $k$ instructions, costing an extra $j$ µs.

Over a block of $k$ instructions the total time is $k\,i + j$, so the effective (average) time per instruction is
$$\frac{k\,i + j}{k} = i + \frac{j}{k}.$$

Equivalently, the page-fault probability per instruction is $1/k$, so the expected time is $i + \frac{1}{k}\cdot j$.

The other options are dimensionally or logically wrong: $i + jk$ and $(i+j)k$ grow with $k$ even though faults get *rarer* as $k$ grows, and $(i+j)/k$ would make the time smaller than one instruction for large $k$.

**Answer: (A)**

es_42fYt4sDptwdWNMt.q:
In a computer system where the ‘best-fit’ algorithm is used for allocating ‘jobs’ to ‘memory partitions’, the following situation was encountered:

When will the \(20\) \(K\) job complete?
es_42fYt4sDptwdWNMt.e:
**Key idea:** these are fixed partitions (4K, 8K, 20K, 2K). Jobs are taken in arrival order, and each one goes into the *smallest free partition that can hold it* (best fit). If no partition fits, the job waits for one to free up.

| Job | Size | Run time |
|---|---|---|
| J1 | 2K | 4 |
| J2 | 14K | 10 |
| J3 | 3K | 2 |
| J4 | 6K | 1 |
| J5 | 6K | 4 |
| J6 | 10K | 1 |
| J7 | 20K | 8 |
| J8 | 2K | 6 |

**Simulation**

- $t=0$: J1 goes to the 2K partition and ends at 4. J2 goes to 20K and ends at 10. J3 goes to 4K and ends at 2. J4 goes to 8K and ends at 1. J5 (6K) needs 8K or 20K, and both are busy, so it waits.
- $t=1$: 8K is free, so J5 goes there and ends at $1+4=5$. J6 (10K) can only fit in 20K, which is busy until 10.
- $t=2,4,5$: the 4K, 2K and 8K partitions free up, but none of them can hold J6 (10K) or J7 (20K).
- $t=10$: J2 leaves 20K. J6 goes there and ends at $11$.
- $t=11$: J7 (20K) goes into 20K and runs for 8 units, ending at $11+8=19$.

J8 (2K) fits in the 2K or 4K partition whenever it is admitted, so it has no effect on J7.

**Answer: The 20K job completes at time 19.**
es_42fYt4sDptwdWNMt.note: The ExamSIDE answer ("after unit time") is not meaningful; simulating best fit over fixed partitions in job order shows the 20K job runs from t = 11 to t = 19.

es_MUw5zpiVCTk8lcP4.q: Which of the following devices should get higher priority in assigning interrupts?
es_MUw5zpiVCTk8lcP4.e:
**Key idea:** interrupt priorities are assigned by *urgency*: how quickly the device must be serviced before data is lost or performance suffers. Fast devices that stream data continuously get the highest priority. Slow, human-paced devices get low priority.

- **(A) Hard disk.** It has the highest data rate. Data streams under the head continuously, so a late response causes buffer overrun or a missed sector, which means a lost revolution. **Highest priority.**
- **(D) Floppy disk.** Also a disk, but much slower than a hard disk, so its priority is lower.
- **(B) Printer.** A slow output device; if it waits a little, nothing is lost.
- **(C) Keyboard.** Very slow, at human typing speed, and keystrokes are buffered by the controller. Servicing it after milliseconds is fine.

So the order of priority is hard disk > floppy > printer/keyboard.

**Answer: (A)**
es_MUw5zpiVCTk8lcP4.note: ExamSIDE lists (C) keyboard, but interrupt priority goes to the fastest device that loses data if serviced late, which is the hard disk.

es_UXxQy8dQugIbOMYP.q:
Consider the following policies for preventing deadlock in a system with mutually exclusive resources.

\(\quad \mathrm{I}.\) \(\quad\) Processes should acquire all their resources at the beginning of execution. If
\(\qquad\) any resource is not available, all resources acquired so far are released
\(\;\; \mathrm{II}.\) \(\quad\) The resources are numbered uniquely, and processes are allowed to request
\(\qquad\) for resources only in increasing resource numbers
\(\;\; \mathrm{III}.\) \(\quad\) The resources are numbered uniquely, and processes are allowed to request
\(\qquad\) for resources only in decreasing resource numbers
\(\;\; \mathrm{IV}.\) \(\quad\) The resources are numbered uniquely. A process is allowed to request only
\(\qquad\) for a resource with resource number larger than its currently held resources

Which of the above policies can be used for preventing deadlock?
o: Any one of \(\mathrm{I}\) and \(\mathrm{III}\) but not \(\mathrm{II}\) or \(\mathrm{IV}\)
Any one of \(\mathrm{I},\) \(\mathrm{III},\) and \(\mathrm{IV}\) but not \(\mathrm{II}\)
Any one of \(\mathrm{II}\) and \(\mathrm{III}\) but not \(\mathrm{I}\) or \(\mathrm{IV}\)
es_UXxQy8dQugIbOMYP.e:
Deadlock prevention works by making one of the four necessary conditions impossible.

- **I.** Acquire everything at the start, and release all if anything is unavailable. A process never holds some resources while waiting for others, so **hold-and-wait** is broken.
- **II.** Request only in increasing resource-number order. A circular wait $P_1 \to P_2 \to \dots \to P_1$ would need resource numbers to strictly increase all the way round the cycle and come back to where they started, which is impossible. **Circular wait** is broken.
- **III.** Decreasing order is the same argument with the order reversed, so circular wait is again impossible.
- **IV.** A process may only request a resource numbered higher than every resource it currently holds. This is the same ordering rule as II, so circular wait is broken.

All four policies prevent deadlock.

**Answer: (D)**

es_WNnywmHAiPqKeefK.q:
A process executes the following code 
for (i = 0; i < n; i + +) fork ( );
The total number of child processes created is
es_WNnywmHAiPqKeefK.e:
**Key idea:** every process alive when `fork()` executes, parent or earlier child, creates one new process. A child continues the loop from the same value of `i` as its parent, so the number of processes **doubles** on each iteration.

| After iteration | Total processes |
|---|---|
| start | $1$ |
| $i=0$ | $2$ |
| $i=1$ | $4$ |
| … | … |
| $i=n-1$ | $2^n$ |

The total at the end is $2^n$, including the original process. The number of **child processes created** is

$$2^n - 1.$$

Check: $n=1$ gives 1 child, and $n=2$ gives 3 children (the parent creates 2, and its first child creates 1).

- **(A) $n$** counts only the original process's direct children.
- **(C) $2^n$** wrongly includes the original process.
- **(D) $2^{n+1}-1$** counts the nodes of a tree with one level too many.

**Answer: (B)**

es_57aekb5tuBZ4uIHs.q:
Which of the following is/are true of the auto-increment addressing mode?
\(\mathrm{I}.\;\;\) It is useful in creating self-relocating code
\(\mathrm{II}.\;\;\) If it is included in an Instruction Set Architecture, then an additional \(ALU\) is required for effective address calculation.
\(\mathrm{III}.\;\;\) The amount of increment depends on the size of the data item accessed
es_57aekb5tuBZ4uIHs.e:
**Key idea:** in auto-increment mode, the register holds the operand's address, and after the access the register is increased by the operand size: `(R)+`.

- **I — False.** Self-relocating (position-independent) code needs addresses relative to something that moves with the code, i.e. PC-relative or base-register addressing. Auto-increment just walks through consecutive data items, which is useful for arrays and stacks, not relocation.
- **II — False.** The increment is a simple "+size" operation. It can be done by the existing ALU or adder (in a later micro-step), or by a small incrementer. No additional full ALU is *required* by the ISA.
- **III — True.** The register is advanced by the size of the item accessed: 1 for a byte, 2 for a halfword, 4 for a word, and so on. This lets it point to the next element.

Only III is true.

**Answer: (C)**

es_oQLzc5bQCiJmJaLI.e:
**Key idea:** the two binary semaphores have different jobs.

- **$X_b$ is a mutex** protecting the shared counter `s`. Every `P(s)` and `V(s)` starts with $P_b(X_b)$ and ends with $V_b(X_b)$, so updates to `s` are atomic. A mutex must start **free**, so $X_b = 1$. If $X_b = 0$, the very first $P_b(X_b)$ would block forever.
- **$Y_b$ is the waiting queue.** A process that drives `s` negative in `P(s)` releases the mutex and blocks on $P_b(Y_b)$. A later `V(s)` that finds waiters ($s \le 0$ after the increment) does $V_b(Y_b)$ to wake exactly one of them. For blocking to work, $Y_b$ must start at **0**. If it were 1, the first process that should block would pass straight through $P_b(Y_b)$ and enter while the semaphore is unavailable.

So the initial values are $X_b = 1$ and $Y_b = 0$.

**Answer: (C)**

es_gmHTq22hxfI7ufpB.q: If the disk in (a) is rotating at \(3600\) rpm, determine the effective data transfer rate which is defined as the number of bytes transferred per second between disk and memory.
es_gmHTq22hxfI7ufpB.e:
The disk from part (a) has $20$ sectors per track. Each sector holds $4000$ bytes of user data plus $96$ bytes of formatting overhead.

**Key idea:** the *effective* transfer rate counts only the data bytes that actually move between the disk and memory. Formatting overhead (gaps, headers, ECC) passes under the head but is not transferred.

**Data per revolution** (one full track):
$$20 \times 4000 = 80{,}000 \text{ bytes}.$$

**Revolutions per second:**
$$\frac{3600}{60} = 60 \text{ rps}.$$

**Effective transfer rate:**
$$80{,}000 \times 60 = 4{,}800{,}000 \text{ bytes/s} \approx 4.8 \text{ MB/s}.$$

If the speed is read as $360$ rpm ($6$ rps), the same method gives $80{,}000 \times 6 = 480{,}000$ bytes/s.

**Answer: 4.8 × 10^6 bytes/s**

es_xNTmbH9csJfFIRJy.q:
If the overhead for formatting a disk is \(96\) bytes for \(40000\) bytes sector, Compute the unformatted capacity of the disk of the following parameters:
Number of surface: \(8\)
Outer diameter of the disk : \(12cm\)
Inner diameter of the disk: \(4cm\)
Inter track space: \(0.1mm\)
Number of sectors per track: \(20\)
es_xNTmbH9csJfFIRJy.e:
**Tracks per surface.** Data is recorded on the annulus between the inner and outer radius:
$$\text{radial width} = \frac{12 - 4}{2} = 4 \text{ cm} = 40 \text{ mm}, \qquad \text{tracks} = \frac{40 \text{ mm}}{0.1 \text{ mm}} = 400.$$

**Unformatted sector size.** The unformatted size includes the formatting overhead:
$$4000 + 96 = 4096 \text{ bytes}.$$

**Unformatted capacity:**
$$8 \text{ surfaces} \times 400 \text{ tracks} \times 20 \text{ sectors} \times 4096 \text{ B} = 64{,}000 \times 4096 = 262{,}144{,}000 \text{ bytes}.$$

That is $\dfrac{262{,}144{,}000}{2^{20}} = 250$ MB.

For comparison, the formatted (usable) capacity is $64{,}000 \times 4000 = 256{,}000{,}000$ bytes.

**Answer: 262,144,000 bytes ≈ 250 MB**

es_1K86RlX5dBqwuTTF.q: The head of a moving head disk with \(100\) tracks numbered \(0\) to \(99\) is currently serving a request at tract \(55.\) If the queue of requests kept in \(FIFO\) order is \(10,70,75,23,65\) Which of the two disk scheduling algorithms \(FCFS\) (First Come First Served) and \(SSTF\) (Shortest Seek Time First) will require less head movement? Find the head movement for each of the algorithms.
es_1K86RlX5dBqwuTTF.e:
The head is at track $55$, and the queue (arrival order) is $10, 70, 75, 23, 65$.

**FCFS** – serve the requests in arrival order:

| Move | Distance |
|---|---|
| 55 → 10 | 45 |
| 10 → 70 | 60 |
| 70 → 75 | 5 |
| 75 → 23 | 52 |
| 23 → 65 | 42 |
| **Total** | **204** |

**SSTF** – always go to the nearest pending track:

| From | Pending distances | Choose | Distance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 55 | 10:45, 70:15, 75:20, 23:32, 65:10 | 65 | 10 |
| 65 | 70:5, 75:10, 23:42, 10:55 | 70 | 5 |
| 70 | 75:5, 23:47, 10:60 | 75 | 5 |
| 75 | 23:52, 10:65 | 23 | 52 |
| 23 | 10:13 | 10 | 13 |
| | | **Total** | **85** |

SSTF needs $85$ tracks of movement against $204$ for FCFS, so **SSTF requires less head movement**.

**Answer: FCFS 204, SSTF 85 – SSTF is better**

es_Xhw3NvvktmqBfaTJ.q:
Which of the following statements are true?
\(\mathrm{I}.\) Shortest remaining time first scheduling may cause starvation
\(\mathrm{II}.\) Preemptive scheduling may cause starvation
\(\mathrm{III}.\) Round robin is better than \(FCFS\) in terms of response time
es_Xhw3NvvktmqBfaTJ.e:
- **I. True.** SRTF always runs the process with the smallest remaining burst. If short jobs keep arriving, a long job can be postponed indefinitely, i.e., it starves.
- **II. True.** Preemptive policies such as preemptive priority scheduling or SRTF let newly arriving "better" processes repeatedly take the CPU away from a low-priority or long process. Starvation is therefore possible. The statement only says *may*, which is enough.
- **III. True.** Round robin gives every ready process a time quantum $q$ in turn. A newly arrived process gets its first CPU slice within about $(n-1)q$, whereas under FCFS it must wait for every earlier process to *finish* its entire burst. Better response time is exactly what RR is designed for.

All three statements are true.

**Answer: (D)**

es_uiY2njg8u111aUFx.q:
Consider the methods used by processes P1 and P2 for accessing their critical sections whenever needed, as given below. The initial values of shared boolean variables S1 and S2 are randomly assigned.


Which of the following statement describes the properties achieved?
es_uiY2njg8u111aUFx.e:
P1 waits while $S1 = S2$, so it enters only when $S1 \ne S2$. P2 waits while $S1 \ne S2$, so it enters only when $S1 = S2$.

**Mutual exclusion holds.** The two entry conditions are complementary, and $S1, S2$ change only in the exit sections:
- P1 exits with $S1 = S2$, which makes the condition true for P2.
- P2 exits with $S2 = \lnot S1$, which makes $S1 \ne S2$ and the condition true for P1.

While one process is inside its critical section, the other only spins and writes nothing, so the other condition can never become true. The two processes can never be inside together.

**Progress fails.** The protocol forces strict alternation P1, P2, P1, … Suppose $S1 \ne S2$ (P1's turn) but P1 does not want to enter its critical section. Then P2 spins forever, even though the critical section is free. A process that is not interested is blocking one that is, which violates progress.

**Answer: (A)**

es_thdxAt1GTy63gCgP.q: The following program consists of 3 concurrent processes and 3 binary semaphores. The semaphores are initialized as S0=1, S1=0, S2=0. How many times will process P0 print '0'?
es_thdxAt1GTy63gCgP.e:
In the original paper, P1 executes `wait(S1); release(S0);` and P2 executes `wait(S2); release(S0);`. All three semaphores are **binary**, so a `release` on a semaphore that is already 1 leaves it at 1 and is effectively lost.

P0 can print once for the initial $S0 = 1$, plus once for each `release(S0)`. P1 and P2 each release S0 at most once, so P0 prints **at most 3** times.

**First print (always):** P0 does `wait(S0)` (S0: 1→0), prints '0', then releases S1 and S2. Now both P1 and P2 can proceed.

**Case 1 – only 2 prints.** P1 runs (S1→0, S0→1), then P2 runs (S2→0, `release(S0)` leaves S0 at 1, so one release is lost). P0 prints a second time and releases S1 and S2, but nobody is left to wait on them. On its next `wait(S0)`, P0 blocks forever. Total **2**.

**Case 2 – 3 prints.** P1 runs (S0→1). P0 prints the second time and releases S1 and S2 (S2 is still 1). P2 then runs (S2→0, S0→1). P0 prints the third time and then blocks. Total **3**.

The count is 2 or 3 depending on the interleaving. That rules out (B), (C) and (D), and P0 always prints **at least twice**.

(If both P1 and P2 waited on S1, no release could be lost and P0 would print exactly three times. The answer depends on P2 waiting on S2.)

**Answer: (A)**

es_SHuvSqyL61j9dyO4.q: A system uses FIFO policy for page replacement. It has \(4\) pages frames with no pages loaded to begin with. The system first accesses \(100\) distinct pages in some order and then accesses the same \(100\) pages but now in the reverse order. How many page faults will occur?
es_SHuvSqyL61j9dyO4.e:
Call the pages $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_{100}$ in the order of the first pass.

**First pass.** All 100 pages are distinct and memory starts empty, so every access faults: **100 faults**.
At the end, the 4 frames hold the last four pages loaded, $p_{97}, p_{98}, p_{99}, p_{100}$, with $p_{97}$ the oldest in FIFO order.

**Reverse pass** ($p_{100}, p_{99}, \dots, p_1$):
- $p_{100}, p_{99}, p_{98}, p_{97}$ are all resident, giving **4 hits**.
- $p_{96}$ is not resident, so it faults and FIFO evicts $p_{97}$. Next $p_{95}$ faults and evicts $p_{98}$, and so on.
- None of $p_{96},\dots,p_1$ is still in memory (each was evicted long ago in the first pass), and once loaded, a page is not referenced again. So each of these 96 accesses is a fault: **96 faults**.

Total page faults $= 100 + 96 = 196$.

**Answer: (A)**

es_ewEEqz5pvOg5r2mx.q: Which of the following is an example of a spooled device?
o: The terminal used to the input data for a program being executed.
The secondary memory device in a virtual memory system.
A line printer used to print the output of a number of jobs.
es_ewEEqz5pvOg5r2mx.e:
**Key idea:** SPOOLing (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line) is used for a **dedicated, non-shareable** device that many jobs want to use. Each job's output is written to a spool area on disk, and a spooler feeds the jobs to the device one at a time. Jobs never wait for the slow device, and their outputs never interleave.

- **(A) Terminal used for input to a running program.** This is interactive and belongs to one session, so it is not spooled.
- **(B) Secondary memory in a virtual memory system.** This is the backing store for paging. It is the *medium* a spooler uses, not a spooled device.
- **(C) Line printer printing the output of several jobs.** This is the textbook example of a spooled device: print files queue on disk and are printed one after another.
- **(D) None of the above.** Wrong, since (C) is a spooled device.

**Answer: (C)**

es_wJD0mJ1BIjNYkcfr.q: At a particular time of computation the value of a counting semaphore is 7. Then 20 P operations and 15 V operations were completed on this semaphore. The resulting value of the semaphore is:
es_wJD0mJ1BIjNYkcfr.e:
For a counting semaphore $S$, each **P** (wait) operation does $S \leftarrow S-1$ and each **V** (signal) operation does $S \leftarrow S+1$.

$$S_{\text{final}} = 7 - 20 + 15 = 2$$

The order in which the operations happened does not change the final value, because every one of them completed. If the value went negative along the way, it only means some processes were blocked for a while and were later woken up by V operations.

**Answer: (B)**

es_TIO1aalrox85nUgQ.q: Which page replacement policy sometimes leads to more page faults when size of memory is increased?
es_TIO1aalrox85nUgQ.e:
**Belady's anomaly:** for some reference strings, *more* frames produce *more* page faults. This can only happen with policies that are not *stack algorithms*.

- **Optimal and LRU are stack algorithms.** The set of pages in memory with $n$ frames is always a subset of the set with $n+1$ frames. So adding frames can never increase faults for these policies.
- **FIFO is not a stack algorithm**, and it shows the anomaly.

Classic string: $1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5$
- With 3 frames, FIFO gives **9** faults.
- With 4 frames, FIFO gives **10** faults.

**Answer: (C)**

es_NWeDD6UkmCecdvs3.q: Let the page reference and the working set window be c c d b c e c e a d and 4, respectively. The initial working set at time \(t=0\) contains the pages {a, d, e}, where a was referenced at time \(t=0,d\) was referenced at time \(t=-1,\) and \(e\) was referenced at time \(t=-2.\) Determine the total number of page faults and the average number of page frames used by computing the working set at each reference.
es_NWeDD6UkmCecdvs3.e:
**Working set with window $\Delta = 4$:** $W(t)$ is the set of distinct pages referenced at times $t-3, \dots, t$. A reference at time $t$ is a page fault if its page is not in $W(t-1)$.

**History before the trace:** $e$ at $t=-2$, $d$ at $t=-1$, $a$ at $t=0$. So $W(0) = \{a,d,e\}$.

| $t$ | Ref | In $W(t-1)$? | Window refs | $W(t)$ | $\lvert W\rvert$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | c | **fault** | e,d,a,c | {a,c,d,e} | 4 |
| 2 | c | hit | d,a,c,c | {a,c,d} | 3 |
| 3 | d | hit | a,c,c,d | {a,c,d} | 3 |
| 4 | b | **fault** | c,c,d,b | {b,c,d} | 3 |
| 5 | c | hit | c,d,b,c | {b,c,d} | 3 |
| 6 | e | **fault** | d,b,c,e | {b,c,d,e} | 4 |
| 7 | c | hit | b,c,e,c | {b,c,e} | 3 |
| 8 | e | hit | c,e,c,e | {c,e} | 2 |
| 9 | a | **fault** | e,c,e,a | {a,c,e} | 3 |
| 10 | d | **fault** | c,e,a,d | {a,c,d,e} | 4 |

- Page faults: at $t = 1, 4, 6, 9, 10$, which gives $5$ faults.
- Average number of frames: $\dfrac{4+3+3+3+3+4+3+2+3+4}{10} = \dfrac{32}{10} = 3.2$.

**Answer: 5 page faults; average 3.2 page frames**

es_ix4KHksb0CuNltD4.q:
Match the pairs in the following question.

List - \(\mathrm{I}\)
\((A)\)\(\;\;\) Virtual Memory
\((B)\)\(\;\;\) Shared memory
\((C)\)\(\;\;\) Look-ahead buffer
\((D)\)\(\;\;\) Look-aside buffer

List - \(\mathrm{II}\)
\((p)\)\(\;\;\) Temporal locality
\((q)\)\(\;\;\) Spatial Locality
\((r)\)\(\;\;\) Address Translation
\((s)\)\(\;\;\) Mutual exclusion
es_ix4KHksb0CuNltD4.e:
**Key idea:** match each mechanism with the principle that makes it work.

- **(A) Virtual memory → (p) temporal locality.** Demand paging works because a program keeps reusing the same pages (its working set) over short periods. Pages brought in therefore stay useful, and page faults remain rare.
- **(B) Shared memory → (s) mutual exclusion.** When several processes read and write a common region, accesses to shared data must be synchronised with locks or semaphores to avoid race conditions.
- **(C) Look-ahead buffer → (q) spatial locality.** A look-ahead (prefetch) buffer fetches the *next* instructions or words before they are requested. This pays off because accesses tend to go to nearby, consecutive addresses.
- **(D) Look-aside buffer → (r) address translation.** The translation look-aside buffer (TLB) caches recent page-to-frame mappings so that virtual-to-physical translation does not need a page-table walk in memory.

**Answer:** A–p, B–s, C–q, D–r

o: It does not ensure the mutual exclusion.
It does not ensure bounded waiting.
It requires that processes enter the critical section in strict alternation
It does not prevent deadlocks, but ensures mutual exclusion
es_j7MGl4fOlNY808ai.e:
**Mutual exclusion holds.** Each process raises its own flag *before* checking the other's. Suppose both were in the critical section. P1 passed its check by reading `wants2 == false`, so P2 had not yet set `wants2`. Then P2 set `wants2` and checked `wants1` *after* P1 had already set `wants1 = true`, so P2 would have spun. That is a contradiction, so the two can never be inside together.

**Deadlock is possible.** Consider this interleaving:

1. P1: `wants1 = true`
2. P2: `wants2 = true`
3. P1 spins on `wants2 == true`, and P2 spins on `wants1 == true`.

Both wait forever, so progress fails.

**Other options**

- **(A) False**, as shown above.
- **(B) False.** Once P2 has raised `wants2`, P1 cannot enter again. When P1 comes back, its check on `wants2` blocks it, so the other process can overtake a waiting process at most once.
- **(C) False.** There is no turn variable. If P2 never wants the critical section (`wants2` stays false), P1 can enter again and again.

So the construct guarantees mutual exclusion but not freedom from deadlock.

**Answer: (D)**

es_UjmczrTTtiw1tsdV.q:
A virtual memory system uses First In First Out (FIFO) page replacement policy and allocates a fixed number of frames to a process. Consider the following statements:
\(P:\) Increasing the number of page frames allocated to a process sometimes increases the page fault rate.
\(Q:\) Some programs do not exhibit locality of reference.

Which one of the following is TRUE?
o: Both P and Q are true, and Q is the reason for P
Both P and Q are true, but Q is not the reason for P.
P is false, but Q is true
Both P and Q are false.
es_UjmczrTTtiw1tsdV.e:
**P is true. This is Belady's anomaly.** With FIFO, adding frames can *increase* the number of faults. Classic example with the string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5: 3 frames give 9 faults, while 4 frames give 10.

**Q is true.** Locality of reference is a typical behaviour, not a law. Some programs, for example those that jump around large data structures randomly or use hashing-heavy access patterns, show little locality.

**Q is not the reason for P.** Belady's anomaly comes from a property of the *replacement algorithm*, not of the program. FIFO is not a **stack algorithm**: the set of pages it keeps in memory with $n$ frames is not always a subset of the set it keeps with $n+1$ frames. The anomaly appears for specific reference strings whether or not the program has locality. Stack algorithms such as LRU and OPT can never show it, even on programs with poor locality.

So both statements are true, but Q does not explain P.

**Answer: (B)**

es_odejfylMjZuCMli3.q:
A process has been allocated \(3\) page frames. Assume that none of the pages of the process are available in the memory initially. The process makes the following sequence of page references (reference string): \[1,2,1,3,7,4,5,6,3,1\]

If optimal page replacement policy is used, how many page faults occur for the above reference string?
es_odejfylMjZuCMli3.e:
**Key idea (optimal / OPT):** on a fault with all frames full, evict the page whose next use is **farthest in the future**, or a page that is never used again.

Reference string: 1, 2, 1, 3, 7, 4, 5, 6, 3, 1 with 3 frames.

| Ref | Frames after | Fault? | Reason for eviction |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | F | |
| 2 | 1 2 | F | |
| 1 | 1 2 | hit | |
| 3 | 1 2 3 | F | |
| 7 | 1 3 7 | F | evict 2 (never used again) |
| 4 | 1 3 4 | F | evict 7 (never used again) |
| 5 | 1 3 5 | F | evict 4 (never used again) |
| 6 | 1 3 6 | F | evict 5 (never used again) |
| 3 | 1 3 6 | hit | |
| 1 | 1 3 6 | hit | |

OPT keeps 1 and 3 resident throughout because they are needed at the end, so the final two references hit.

Faults: 1, 2, 3, 7, 4, 5, 6, which is **7 page faults**.

**Answer: (A)**

es_q0U1tEZjxSvxF2o2.q:
A process has been allocated \(3\) page frames. Assume that none of the pages of the process are available in the memory initially. The process makes the following sequence of page references (reference string): \[1,2,1,3,7,4,5,6,3,1\]

Least Recently Used (LRU) page replacement policy is a practical approximation to optimal page replacement. For the above reference string, how many more page faults occur with LRU than with the optimal page replacement policy?
es_q0U1tEZjxSvxF2o2.e:
**Key idea:** count the faults under LRU and under OPT for the same string, then subtract.

Reference string: 1, 2, 1, 3, 7, 4, 5, 6, 3, 1 with 3 frames.

**LRU:** on a fault with all frames full, evict the page used **least recently**. The "recency order" column lists pages from least to most recently used.

| Ref | Recency order after (LRU → MRU) | Fault? | Evicted |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | F | |
| 2 | 1 2 | F | |
| 1 | 2 1 | hit | |
| 3 | 2 1 3 | F | |
| 7 | 1 3 7 | F | 2 |
| 4 | 3 7 4 | F | 1 |
| 5 | 7 4 5 | F | 3 |
| 6 | 4 5 6 | F | 7 |
| 3 | 5 6 3 | F | 4 |
| 1 | 6 3 1 | F | 5 |

LRU gives **9 faults**. The long run of new pages (7, 4, 5, 6) pushes out 1 and 3 just before they are needed again.

**OPT:** evict the page used farthest in the future. OPT keeps 1 and 3 resident and rotates 7, 4, 5, 6 through the third frame, so the final 3 and 1 are hits. It gives **7 faults** (1, 2, 3, 7, 4, 5, 6).

**Difference:** $9 - 7 = 2$ more faults with LRU.

**Answer: (C)**

es_9spo16WSwEZgQ11Y.q: A computer has six tape drives, with n processes competing for them. Each process may need two drives. What is the maximum value of n for the system to be deadlock free?
es_9spo16WSwEZgQ11Y.e:
**Key idea:** consider the worst case — every process grabs one drive and then waits for its second. Deadlock is possible only if *all* drives can be handed out this way while every process still needs one more.

With $R$ identical resources and $n$ processes each needing at most $m$ of them, the system is deadlock-free iff
$$n(m-1) + 1 \le R.$$

Here $m = 2$, $R = 6$: $n(2-1) + 1 \le 6 \Rightarrow n \le 5$.

Check:
- $n = 5$: worst case each of the 5 processes holds 1 drive → 5 drives used, **1 still free**. Some process gets it, finishes, releases 2 drives, and the rest can then finish. No deadlock.
- $n = 6$: each of the 6 processes can hold 1 drive → all 6 drives used, every process waits for a second drive that will never be released → **deadlock**.

So the maximum $n$ is 5.

**Answer: (B)**

es_pMEBlIZhKHnzoyuG.q: A uni-processor computer system only has two processes, both of which alternate \(10\) \(ms\) \(CPU\) bursts with \(90\) \(ms\) \(\mathrm{I}/O\) bursts. Both the processes were created at nearly the same time. The \(\mathrm{I}/O\) of both processes can proceed in parallel. Which of the following scheduling strategies will result in the least \(CPU\) utilization (over a long period of time) for this system?
o: Static priority scheduling with different priorities for the two processes
Round robin scheduling with a time quantum of \(5\) \(ms.\)
es_pMEBlIZhKHnzoyuG.e:
**Key idea:** each process needs 10 ms of CPU per cycle, so CPU utilization depends on how long one cycle (CPU burst + 90 ms I/O) takes. Anything that delays the *completion* of a CPU burst delays the start of the I/O and stretches the cycle.

**FCFS, SRTF, static priority** (both bursts equal, so all three behave the same):
- 0–10: P1 runs; 10–20: P2 runs.
- P1's I/O: 10–100; P2's I/O: 20–110.
- 100–110: P1; 110–120: P2; … repeating every **100 ms**.
- Utilization $= 20/100 = 20\%$.

**Round robin, $q = 5$ ms:**
- 0–5 P1, 5–10 P2, 10–15 P1 (burst done), 15–20 P2 (burst done).
- P1's I/O: 15–105; P2's I/O: 20–110.
- 105–110 P1; at 110 P2 returns (queued ahead of the preempted P1): 110–115 P2, 115–120 P1 (done), 120–125 P2 (done).
- P1's bursts end at 15, 120, 225, … → cycle of **105 ms**.
- Utilization $= 20/105 \approx 19\%$.

Interleaving the bursts makes *both* processes finish their CPU bursts later, so both start I/O later and the CPU idles longer. In addition, RR performs a context switch every 5 ms — pure overhead that the other policies avoid. Hence RR gives the **least** CPU utilization.

**Answer: (D)**

o: P(S) at W, V(S) at X, P(T) at Y, V(T) at Z, S and T initially 1
P(S) at W, V(T) at X, P(T) at Y,  V(S) at Z, S initially 1 and T initially 0
P(S) at W, V(T) at X, P(T) at Y,V(T) at Z, S and T initially 1
P(S) at W, V(S) at X, P(T) at Y,  V(T) at Z, S initially 1 and T initially 0
es_FMQyWxqOJglu5x55.e:
**Key idea:** the output `001100110011…` needs **strict alternation** P, Q, P, Q, … with P going first. Use two semaphores as "turn" signals: P waits on S and hands over to Q through T; Q waits on T and hands back through S. Start with S = 1 (P may go) and T = 0 (Q must wait).

**Option (B):** P(S) at W, V(T) at X, P(T) at Y, V(S) at Z; S = 1, T = 0.

| Step | Action | S | T | Output so far |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| start | – | 1 | 0 | – |
| P | P(S), prints `00`, V(T) | 0 | 1 | `00` |
| P again | P(S) blocks (S = 0) | 0 | 1 | |
| Q | P(T), prints `11`, V(S) | 1 | 0 | `0011` |
| P | P(S), prints `00`, V(T) | 0 | 1 | `001100` |

Q cannot go first because T = 0, and neither process can run twice in a row. The output is therefore always `001100110011…`.

**Why the others fail**

- **(A)** S and T are independent and each process only waits on its own semaphore. P and Q run concurrently with no ordering, so `0101…` or `11…` first is possible.
- **(C)** T = 1 initially, so Q can print `11` first. Also, S is never signalled, so P runs only once.
- **(D)** T = 0 and only Q touches T, so Q blocks forever and the output is `0000…`.

**Answer: (B)**

es_NGFmz8qRDg8INQTF.q:
Consider the \(3\) processes, \(P1,\) \(P2\) and \(P3\) shown in the table.
Process Arrival Time Time Units
Required
P1 0 5
P2 1 7
P3 3 4

The completion order of the \(3\) processes under the policies \(FCFS\) and \(RR2\) (round robin scheduling with \(CPU\) quantum of \(2\) time units) are
es_NGFmz8qRDg8INQTF.e:

**RR with quantum 2.** New arrivals join the queue tail. A preempted process is re-queued at the tail when its quantum ends.

| Time | Runs | Remaining after | Ready queue after |

| 0–2 | P1 | P1:3 | P2 (arrived at 1), P1 |

es_31zpyfft8GA1Ee0p.q:
Consider the virtual page reference string \[1,2,3,2,4,1,3,2,4,1\]
On a demand paged virtual memory system running on a computer system that has main memory size of \(3\) page frames which are initially empty. Let \(LRU,\) \(FIFO\) and \(OPTIMAL\) denote the number of page faults under the corresponding page replacement policy. Then
es_31zpyfft8GA1Ee0p.e:
The reference string is $1,2,3,2,4,1,3,2,4,1$ with 3 frames. F = fault, H = hit.

**FIFO**
1F, 2F, 3F $[1,2,3]$; 2H; 4F (evict 1) $[2,3,4]$; 1F (evict 2) $[3,4,1]$; 3H; 2F (evict 3) $[4,1,2]$; 4H; 1H.
FIFO $=6$ faults.

**LRU**
1F, 2F, 3F; 2H; 4F (evict 1, the least recent) $[2,3,4]$; 1F (evict 3) $[2,4,1]$; 3F (evict 2) $[4,1,3]$; 2F (evict 4) $[1,3,2]$; 4F (evict 1) $[3,2,4]$; 1F (evict 3).
LRU $=9$ faults. The string keeps re-referencing exactly the page LRU has just thrown out.

**OPTIMAL**
1F, 2F, 3F; 2H.
4F: the next uses are 1 at position 6, 3 at 7 and 2 at 8, so evict 2, giving $[1,3,4]$.
1H; 3H.
2F: 3 is never used again, so evict 3, giving $[1,4,2]$.
4H; 1H.
OPTIMAL $=5$ faults.

$5 < 6 < 9$, so OPTIMAL < FIFO < LRU.

**Answer: (B)**

es_O5O0yCLk9u5rmRu4.q: A file system with 300 G Byte disk uses a file descriptor with 8 direct block addresses, 1 indirect block address and 1 doubly indirect block address. The size of each disk block is 128 Bytes and the size of each disk block address is 8 Bytes. The maximum possible file size in this file system is
o: dependent on the size of the disk
es_O5O0yCLk9u5rmRu4.e:
Addresses per block $= \dfrac{128 \text{ B}}{8 \text{ B}} = 16$.

Number of data blocks reachable from one file descriptor:
- 8 direct pointers give $8$ blocks;
- 1 single-indirect pointer gives $16$ blocks;
- 1 double-indirect pointer gives $16 \times 16 = 256$ blocks.

Total $= 8 + 16 + 256 = 280$ blocks.

Maximum file size $= 280 \times 128 \text{ B} = 35840 \text{ B} = 35$ KB.

The disk size does not limit this. A 300 GB disk has about $2.3\times 10^{9}$ blocks of 128 B, which an 8-byte address can easily name. The bottleneck is the descriptor structure, so (D) is wrong. (C) mistakes 280 blocks for 280 KB.

**Answer: (B)**

es_0BrAsshuZYXjyJ8Z.q:
A computer system has 6 tape drives, with n process completing for them.
Each process may need 3 tape drives. The maximum value of n for which the
