go_v3_5.20.25.q:
Recall that Belady's anomaly is that the page-fault rate may *increase* as the number of allocated frames increases. Now, consider the following statements:

- $S_1$: *Random page replacement* algorithm (where a page chosen at random is replaced) suffers from Belady's anomaly.
- $S_2$: *LRU page replacement* algorithm suffers from Belady's anomaly.

Which of the following is CORRECT?
go_v3_5.20.25.e:
**Key idea:** a *stack algorithm* is one where, for every reference string, the set of pages in memory with $n$ frames is always a subset of the set with $n+1$ frames. Stack algorithms can never show Belady's anomaly. LRU and OPT are stack algorithms; FIFO and Random are not.

**$S_2$ is false.** With $n$ frames, LRU holds exactly the $n$ most recently used distinct pages. These are always a subset of the $n+1$ most recently used pages. So every hit with $n$ frames is also a hit with $n+1$ frames, and adding a frame can never increase the number of faults.

**$S_1$ is true.** Random replacement has no inclusion property. The victim is chosen at random, so one possible run makes exactly the choices FIFO would make (always evicting the oldest page). Take the classic reference string
$$1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5$$
If the random choices happen to match FIFO, the run gives $9$ faults with $3$ frames but $10$ faults with $4$ frames. So random replacement can suffer from Belady's anomaly.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v3_5.20.29.q:
The address sequence generated by tracing a particular program executing in a pure demand paging system with $100$ bytes per page is
$$0100, 0200, 0430, 0499, 0510, 0530, 0560, 0120, 0220, 0240, 0260, 0320, 0410.$$
Suppose that the memory can store only one page and if $x$ is the address which causes a page fault then the bytes from addresses $x$ to $x + 99$ are loaded on to the memory.
How many page faults will occur?
go_v3_5.20.29.e:
**Key idea:** the single "page" in memory is the window $[x,\,x+99]$ that starts at the faulting address. It is not an aligned block such as $0$–$99$ or $100$–$199$. An address is a hit only if it falls inside the current window.

| Address | In current window? | Result | Window after |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0100 | — (memory empty) | fault 1 | 100–199 |
| 0200 | no | fault 2 | 200–299 |
| 0430 | no | fault 3 | 430–529 |
| 0499 | yes | hit | 430–529 |
| 0510 | yes | hit | 430–529 |
| 0530 | no ($> 529$) | fault 4 | 530–629 |
| 0560 | yes | hit | 530–629 |
| 0120 | no | fault 5 | 120–219 |
| 0220 | no ($> 219$) | fault 6 | 220–319 |
| 0240 | yes | hit | 220–319 |
| 0260 | yes | hit | 220–319 |
| 0320 | no ($> 319$) | fault 7 | 320–419 |
| 0410 | yes | hit | 320–419 |

There are **7** page faults.

Option D ($8$) is what aligned 100-byte pages would give, with page numbers $1,2,4,4,5,5,5,1,2,2,2,3,4$. The question explicitly loads $x$ to $x+99$ instead.

**Answer: (C)**

go_v3_5.20.30.q: A demand paging system takes $100$ time units to service a page fault and $300$ time units to replace a dirty page. Memory access time is $1$ time unit. The probability of a page fault is $p$. In case of a page fault, the probability of page being dirty is also $p$. It is observed that the average access time is $3$ time units. Then the value of $p$ is
go_v3_5.20.30.e:
**Key idea:** weight the time of each case by its probability.

| Case | Probability | Time |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| No page fault | $1-p$ | $1$ |
| Fault, page not dirty | $p(1-p)$ | $100$ |
| Fault, dirty page replaced | $p\cdot p$ | $300$ |

$$3 = (1-p)\cdot 1 + p(1-p)\cdot 100 + p^2\cdot 300 = 1 + 99p + 200p^2$$
$$200p^2 + 99p - 2 = 0$$
$$p = \frac{-99 + \sqrt{99^2 + 1600}}{400} = \frac{-99 + \sqrt{11401}}{400} \approx \frac{7.775}{400} \approx 0.0194$$
The other root is negative.

**Matching the options.** The exact value is $p \approx 0.0194$, and only option A has these digits; it is the intended answer with a misplaced decimal point.
- Plugging $p = 0.194$ into the formula gives about $27.7$ time units, not $3$.
- Options B, C and D give even larger times.
- Other reasonable models give $p \approx 0.019$ as well: charging the 1-unit access in every case gives $\approx 0.0193$, and treating a dirty fault as $100 + 300$ units gives $\approx 0.0191$.

**Answer: (A)** (exact value $p \approx 0.0194$)

go_v3_5.20.31.q:
Assume that a main memory with only $4$ pages, each of $16$ bytes, is initially empty. The CPU generates the following sequence of virtual addresses and uses the Least Recently Used (LRU) page replacement policy.
$$0, 4, 8, 20, 24, 36, 44, 12, 68, 72, 80, 84, 28, 32, 88, 92$$
How many page faults does this sequence cause? What are the page numbers of the pages present in the main memory at the end of the sequence?
go_v3_5.20.31.e:
**Step 1: convert addresses to page numbers.** Page number $= \lfloor \text{address}/16 \rfloor$.

| Addresses | 0, 4, 8 | 20, 24 | 36, 44 | 12 | 68, 72 | 80, 84 | 28 | 32 | 88, 92 |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Page | 0 | 1 | 2 | 0 | 4 | 5 | 1 | 2 | 5 |

Immediately repeated pages are always hits, so the effective reference string is $0, 1, 2, 0, 4, 5, 1, 2, 5$.

**Step 2: run LRU with 4 frames.** The frames are listed from least to most recently used.

| Ref | Result | Victim | Frames (LRU → MRU) |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 | fault 1 | – | 0 |
| 1 | fault 2 | – | 0 1 |
| 2 | fault 3 | – | 0 1 2 |
| 0 | hit | – | 1 2 0 |
| 4 | fault 4 | – | 1 2 0 4 |
| 5 | fault 5 | 1 | 2 0 4 5 |
| 1 | fault 6 | 2 | 0 4 5 1 |
| 2 | fault 7 | 0 | 4 5 1 2 |
| 5 | hit | – | 4 1 2 5 |

There are **7** page faults, and the final contents are pages **1, 2, 4, 5**.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v3_5.21.1.q:
Consider the following precedence graph ($\text{Fig. } 6$) of processes where a node denotes a process and a directed edge from node $P_i$ to node $P_j$ implies; that $P_i$ must complete before $P_j$ commences. Implement the graph using FORK and JOIN constructs. The actual computation done by a process may be indicated by a comment line.

**Figure (Fig. 6): directed edges of the precedence graph**

$P_1 \to P_2,\quad P_1 \to P_3,\quad P_1 \to P_4,\quad P_2 \to P_4,\quad P_2 \to P_5,\quad P_3 \to P_5,\quad P_4 \to P_6,\quad P_5 \to P_6$
go_v3_5.21.1.e:
**Constructs used**
- `fork L` starts a new concurrent flow of control at label `L`, and the parent continues with the next statement.
- `join count` is executed atomically as `count := count - 1; if count ≠ 0 then quit;`. Of the `count` flows that reach a join, only the last one to arrive continues.

**Analysing the graph** (predecessors of each node)

| Process | Must wait for |
|---|---|
| $P_2$, $P_3$ | $P_1$ |
| $P_4$ | $P_1, P_2$ (the edge $P_1\to P_4$ is already implied by $P_1\to P_2\to P_4$) |
| $P_5$ | $P_2, P_3$, a join of 2 flows |
| $P_6$ | $P_4, P_5$, a join of 2 flows |

**Program**
```
        count5 := 2;        /* P5 waits for P2 and P3 */
        count6 := 2;        /* P6 waits for P4 and P5 */
        /* P1 : computation of P1 */
        fork L3;            /* P3 may start as soon as P1 is over */
        /* P2 : computation of P2 */
        fork L4;            /* P4 may start as soon as P2 is over */
        goto L5;
L3:     /* P3 : computation of P3 */
L5:     join count5;        /* last of the {P2, P3} flows survives */
        /* P5 : computation of P5 */
        goto L6;
L4:     /* P4 : computation of P4 */
L6:     join count6;        /* last of the {P4, P5} flows survives */
        /* P6 : computation of P6 */
```

**Checking the program**
- P2 and P3 both start only after P1, and they run concurrently.
- P4 is forked only after P2, which itself ran after P1.
- The main flow (after P2) and the P3 flow both reach `join count5`. Whichever arrives first quits, and the second one runs P5. So P5 runs only after both P2 and P3.
- The P4 flow and the P5 flow both reach `join count6`. Only the last one continues to P6, so P6 runs after both P4 and P5.

No constraint is missing, and no extra waiting is added, so maximum concurrency is preserved.

A plain parbegin/parend program cannot express this graph exactly. It contains the "N" pattern $P_3\to P_5 \leftarrow P_2 \to P_4$ with $P_3$ and $P_4$ unrelated, so the graph is not properly nested. That is why fork/join is needed here.

**Answer: P1; fork L3; P2; fork L4; goto L5; L3: P3; L5: join count5; P5; goto L6; L4: P4; L6: join count6; P6 (with count5 = count6 = 2)**

go_v3_5.21.2.q: A given set of processes can be implemented by using only **parbegin/parend** statement, if the precedence graph of these processes is ______
go_v3_5.21.2.e:
**Key idea:** parbegin/parend (cobegin/coend) can combine computations in only two ways, and these can be nested:
- **in sequence:** `S1; S2`
- **in parallel:** `parbegin S1; S2; ...; Sn parend`

So the precedence graphs it can express are exactly those built recursively from single processes by series and parallel composition. These are the **properly nested** (series–parallel) graphs.

*Expressible example:* $P_1 \to \{P_2, P_3\} \to P_4$ is written as
`P1; parbegin P2; P3 parend; P4`.

*Not expressible:* the "N"-shaped pattern $a\to c,\; b\to c,\; b\to d$, with $a$ and $d$ unrelated.
- If $a$ and $b$ are put in one parbegin block followed by $c$ and $d$, then $d$ is forced to wait for $a$. That adds a constraint and loses concurrency.
- Any other arrangement breaks one of the required orderings.

Graphs like this need fork/join (or semaphores) instead.

**Answer: properly nested**

go_v3_5.21.3.q:
Draw the precedence graph for the concurrent program given below

```
S1
parbegin
   begin
      S2:S4
   end;
   begin
      S3;
      parbegin
         S5;
         begin
            S6:S8
         end
      parend
   end;
   S7
parend;
S9
```
go_v3_5.21.3.e:
**Key idea:** in `parbegin C1; C2; …; Cn parend`, all components start together once the statement before `parbegin` has finished. The statement after `parend` starts only when every component has finished. Statements inside `begin … end` run one after another, so `S2:S4` means S2 followed by S4, and `S6:S8` means S6 followed by S8.

**Structure of the program**
- S1 runs first.
- The outer `parbegin` has three concurrent branches:
  1. S2 ; S4
  2. S3 ; then an inner `parbegin` of { S5 ∥ (S6 ; S8) }
  3. S7
- S9 runs after the outer `parend`, i.e. after all three branches are complete.

**Edges of the precedence graph**

| From | To |
|---|---|
| S1 | S2, S3, S7 |
| S2 | S4 |
| S3 | S5, S6 |
| S6 | S8 |
| S4 | S9 |
| S5 | S9 |
| S8 | S9 |

The process state transition diagram of an operating system is as given below.

Which of the following must be FALSE about the above operating system?

**Figure** (states: Start, Ready, Running, Blocked, Terminated). The diagram has exactly these transitions:
- Start → Ready, labelled "Create a new process"
- Ready → Running, labelled "Schedule"
- Running → Terminated, labelled "Exit"
- Running → Blocked, labelled "Wait for I/O completion or resource released"
- Blocked → Ready, labelled "I/O complete or resource released"
o: It is a multiprogrammed operating system
It is a multi-user operating system
go_v3_5.22.5.e:
With **preemptive** scheduling the OS can take the CPU away from a running process (timer interrupt at the end of a time slice, or arrival of a higher-priority process) and put it back into the ready queue. That requires a **Running → Ready** transition. The diagram has no such edge: a running process gives up the CPU only voluntarily — by exiting or by blocking for I/O or a resource. Hence the OS cannot be using preemptive scheduling, so (B) must be false.

- (C) Non-preemptive scheduling is exactly what the diagram shows.

go_v3_5.23.2.q:
State any undesirable characteristic of the following criteria for measuring performance of an operating system:

**Waiting time**
go_v3_5.23.2.e:
**Waiting time** of a process is the total time it spends in the *ready queue* waiting for the CPU (for a pure CPU job, turnaround time − burst time). Using it (usually its average) as the yardstick of an OS has these drawbacks:

1. **It favours short jobs and permits starvation.** Average waiting time is minimised by Shortest-Job-First (SRTF when preemptive). A scheduler tuned for this criterion keeps postponing long jobs; a long job can wait indefinitely while the *average* still looks excellent. The criterion says nothing about fairness or about the spread (variance) of waiting times.
2. **It is not what an interactive user experiences.** It counts only time in the ready queue — not the time until the first response, not time blocked for I/O, not service time. A small average waiting time does not guarantee good response time.
3. **It is not normalised to job length.** Long jobs naturally accumulate more waiting (e.g. under round robin), so raw waiting times of short and long jobs are not comparable.
4. **It is hard to optimise in practice**, because minimising it needs the CPU-burst lengths in advance, which are unknown and can only be estimated.

**Answer: Optimising (average) waiting time favours short processes (SJF-like) and can starve long ones; it ignores response time, I/O waiting and fairness.**

go_v3_5.23.46.q:
In the working-set strategy, which of the following is done by the operating system to prevent thrashing?

I. It initiates another process if there are enough extra frames.

II. It selects a process to suspend if the sum of the sizes of the working-sets exceeds the total number of available frames.
go_v3_5.23.46.e:
In the working-set model the OS tracks, for every process, its working set $WS_i$ (the pages referenced in the last $\Delta$ references) and the total demand $D = \sum_i |WS_i|$. Thrashing occurs when $D > m$, the number of available frames: some process cannot keep its working set in memory and faults continually.

The OS policy is:
- if $D < m$, there are enough extra frames, so the OS may **initiate (admit) another process**, raising the degree of multiprogramming and CPU utilisation — statement I;
- if $D > m$, the OS **selects a process to suspend** (swap out), and its frames are given to the others; it is resumed later — statement II.

This keeps the degree of multiprogramming as high as possible while preventing thrashing, so both statements describe the strategy.

**Answer: (D)**

go_v3_5.23.48.q: Consider $n$ jobs $J_1, J_2 \ldots J_n$ such that job $J_i$ has execution time $t_i$ and a non-negative integer weight $w_i$. The weighted mean completion time of the jobs is defined to be $\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i T_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i}$, where $T_i$ is the completion time of job $J_i$. Assuming that there is only one processor available, in what order must the jobs be executed in order to minimize the weighted mean completion time of the jobs?
go_v3_5.23.48.e:
The denominator $\sum w_i$ does not depend on the order, so we must minimise $\sum w_i T_i$. Use an **exchange argument** on two adjacent jobs $a$ then $b$ that start at time $s$; swapping them affects no other job.

- Order $a, b$: $\;w_a(s + t_a) + w_b(s + t_a + t_b)$
- Order $b, a$: $\;w_b(s + t_b) + w_a(s + t_a + t_b)$

Difference (first − second) $= w_b t_a - w_a t_b$. So $a$ should precede $b$ iff $w_b t_a \le w_a t_b$, i.e. $\dfrac{w_a}{t_a} \ge \dfrac{w_b}{t_b}$.

Any schedule with an adjacent pair out of this order can be improved (or kept equal) by swapping the pair, so an optimal schedule runs the jobs in **non-increasing order of $w_i/t_i$** (Smith's ratio rule).

Why the others fail:
- (A) Shortest-first is optimal only when all weights are equal: for $J_1 = (t{=}1, w{=}1)$, $J_2 = (t{=}2, w{=}10)$ it gives $1 + 10\cdot 3 = 31$, while $J_2$ first gives $10\cdot 2 + 1\cdot 3 = 23$.
- (B), (C) ignore how long a heavy job delays the others: for $J_1 = (1, 1)$, $J_2 = (10, 2)$ both put $J_2$ first, giving $2\cdot 10 + 1\cdot 11 = 31$, while $J_1$ first gives $1 + 2\cdot 11 = 23$.

**Answer: (D)**

go_v3_5.23.49.q: If the time-slice used in the round-robin scheduling policy is more than the maximum time required to execute any process, then the policy will
o: degenerate to first come first serve
go_v3_5.23.49.e:
Round robin takes the process at the head of a FIFO ready queue and lets it run for at most one time quantum $q$; a process that has not finished is preempted and appended to the tail.

If $q$ is larger than the CPU time needed by any process, **no process is ever preempted**: the process at the head of the queue completes within its first quantum, then the next process in queue (arrival) order runs to completion, and so on. That is exactly non-preemptive **first-come-first-served**. Burst length and priority never influence the order, so it is neither SJF nor priority scheduling.

**Answer: (C)**

go_v3_5.24.2.e:
**Roles of the variables.** `ar` = readers that have requested access and not yet finished (waiting or reading); `rr` = readers that have been *granted* access (`V(reading)` done for them) and not yet finished; `aw`, `rw` = the same for writers. All counters are updated inside `P(mutex) … V(mutex)`. `grantread` admits **all** pending readers, but only if no writer is present ($aw = 0$); `grantwrite` admits **all** pending writers if no reader holds access ($rr = 0$). (The writer's statement `ar := aw - 1` is evidently a misprint for `aw := aw - 1`; read literally, `aw` would never decrease and readers would be shut out for ever after the first write.)

**(a)** A `V(reading)` / `V(writing)` is issued only for a process that is about to execute (or is blocked in) the matching `P`, so once every admitted process is inside, both semaphores have value 0; `mutex` is 1 whenever nobody is updating the counters.
- *12 readers reading, nobody waiting:* $ar = rr = 12$, $aw = rw = 0$; mutex $= 1$, reading $= 0$, writing $= 0$; no process is blocked. (If $w$ writers have arrived meanwhile: $aw = w$, $rw = 0$ and they are blocked on `writing`; readers arriving after them are blocked on `reading` and counted only in `ar`, so $ar = 12 +$ (number of blocked readers) while $rr = 12$.)
- *Writers writing:* $rr = 0$, $aw = rw =$ number of writers admitted (this scheme admits all of them at once), $ar =$ number of readers blocked on `reading`; mutex $= 1$, reading $= 0$, writing $= 0$.

**(b)** *Readers cannot starve writers.* As soon as a writer arrives, $aw > 0$, so `grantread` admits no further reader. The readers already admitted finish, and the last one (making $rr = 0$) calls `grantwrite`, which admits the waiting writer(s).

*Writers can starve readers.* Readers are admitted only when $aw = 0$. If writers keep arriving — each new writer is admitted immediately because $rr = 0$ — $aw$ never returns to 0 and the waiting readers never get `V(reading)`.

**(c)** `grantwrite` performs `V(writing)` for **every** waiting writer (`while rw < aw`), and a writer arriving while others are writing is also admitted at once because $rr = 0$. Hence several writers can write simultaneously — writers are not mutually exclusive with one another — so the solution is incorrect.

(A fix: admit a writer only when $rr = 0$ **and** $rw = 0$, one at a time, and let a finishing writer call `grantwrite` before `grantread`.)

**Answer: (a) 12 readers reading: $ar = rr = 12$, $aw = rw = 0$, mutex $= 1$, reading $=$ writing $= 0$; (b) readers cannot starve writers, but writers can starve readers; (c) `grantwrite` admits all waiting writers at once, so several writers can write together.**

go_v3_5.24.3.q:
Given below is solution for the critical section problem of two processes $P_0$ and $P_1$ sharing the following variables:

```pascal
var flag :array [0..1] of boolean; (initially false)
    turn: 0 .. 1;
```

The program below is for process $P_i\ (i = 0 \text{ or } 1)$ where process $P_j\ (j = 1 \text{ or } 0)$ being the other one.

```pascal
repeat
    flag[i]:= true;
    while turn != i
    do begin
        while flag [j] do skip
        turn:=i;
    end

    critical section

    flag[i]:=false;
until false
```

Determine if the above solution is correct. If it is incorrect, demonstrate with an example how it violates the conditions.
go_v3_5.24.3.e:
The solution (Hyman's algorithm) is **incorrect**: it violates **mutual exclusion**. The flaw is that a process can get past the test `while flag[j]` and then be delayed before it executes `turn := i`; meanwhile the other process, whose turn it still is, walks straight in.

Counter-example — initially `flag[0] = flag[1] = false`, `turn = 0`:

| Step | $P_0$ | $P_1$ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | | `flag[1] := true` |
| 2 | | `turn != 1`, so it enters the loop body; `while flag[0]` finds `flag[0] = false` and falls through; **preempted just before `turn := 1`** |
| 3 | `flag[0] := true` | |
| 4 | `while turn != 0` is false (turn = 0), so **enters the CS** | |
| 5 | (still in CS) | `turn := 1`; `while turn != 1` is now false, so **enters the CS** |

Both processes are in the critical section at the same time.

It also fails **bounded waiting**: while `turn = 0`, $P_0$ can leave (`flag[0] := false`) and immediately re-enter (`flag[0] := true`; `turn = 0`, so no waiting) again and again, while $P_1$ spins in `while flag[0] do skip` and may never observe the brief moments when `flag[0]` is false — $P_1$ can starve. (Progress does hold: a process that wants to enter while the other is not interested finds `flag[j]` false, sets `turn := i` and enters.)

**Answer: The solution is incorrect — both processes can be inside the critical section simultaneously (mutual exclusion violated, as in the trace above); bounded waiting also fails.**

go_v3_5.24.5.e:
**Yes, mutual exclusion is guaranteed.**

Key observation: $P_i$ leaves the `while` loop (and enters the CS) only when it finds `flag[j]` and `flag[k]` both false, and at that moment its own `flag[i]` is true — each back-off branch sets `flag[i] := true` again before the loop condition is re-tested. `flag[i]` then stays true until $P_i$ leaves the CS.

Suppose $P_i$ and $P_j$ were in the CS together. Let $s_i$ be the time $P_i$ last set `flag[i] := true` and $t_i > s_i$ the time it read `flag[j] = false`; define $s_j < t_j$ in the same way for $P_j$ (which read `flag[i] = false`).
- `flag[j]` is true from $s_j$ until $P_j$ leaves the CS, so $P_i$ can have read it as false only earlier: $t_i < s_j$.
- In the same way $t_j < s_i$.

Then $s_i < t_i < s_j < t_j < s_i$ — a contradiction. The same argument applies to every pair of processes, so at most one process is in the CS at any time.

The variable `turn` only decides which process backs off under contention; it is not needed for safety. (The scheme does have a liveness problem — a waiting process can be blocked for ever — which is the subject of part (b).)

**Answer: Yes — mutual exclusion is ensured: a process enters only after raising its own flag and then seeing both other flags false, which two processes cannot both do.**

go_v3_5.24.7.q:
Write a concurrent program using **parbegin-parend** and semaphores to represent the precedence constraints of the statements $S_1$ to $S_6$, as shown in figure below.

**Figure** (precedence graph; $X \to Y$ means $X$ must complete before $Y$ starts):
- $S_1 \to S_2$, $\;S_1 \to S_3$
- $S_2 \to S_4$, $\;S_2 \to S_5$
- $S_3 \to S_5$
- $S_6 \to S_4$, $\;S_6 \to S_5$

go_v3_5.24.8.q:
(A) Draw a precedence graph for the following sequential code. The statements are numbered from $S_1$ to $S_6$

```text
S1    read n
S2    i := 1
S3    if i > n next
S4    a(i) := i+1
S5    i := i+1
S6    next : write a(i)
```

(B) Can this graph be converted to a concurrent program using parbegin-parend construct only?
go_v3_5.24.8.e:
**(A)** Two statements can run concurrently only if neither writes a variable that the other reads or writes (Bernstein's conditions). Read/write sets:

| Statement | Reads | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| $S_1$: read n | — | n |
| $S_2$: i := 1 | — | i |
| $S_3$: if i > n goto next | i, n | — (decides whether $S_4, S_5$ run) |
| $S_4$: a(i) := i+1 | i | a(i) |
| $S_5$: i := i+1 | i | i |
| $S_6$: write a(i) | i, a | — |

Dependencies:
- $S_1 \to S_3$ (n) and $S_2 \to S_3$ (i); $S_1$ and $S_2$ share no variable, so they are independent.
- $S_3 \to S_4$ and $S_3 \to S_5$: both execute only if the test fails (control dependence).
- $S_4 \to S_5$: $S_4$ reads i and $S_5$ writes i (anti-dependence), so they cannot overlap.
- $S_5 \to S_6$: $S_6$ must use the new value of i (and the array after $S_4$). If the jump is taken, $S_6$ simply follows $S_3$.

Precedence graph (transitive edges such as $S_2 \to S_4$ or $S_3 \to S_6$ omitted):

$$S_1 \to S_3,\qquad S_2 \to S_3,\qquad S_3 \to S_4 \to S_5 \to S_6$$

that is, $S_1$ and $S_2$ in parallel, followed by the chain $S_3, S_4, S_5, S_6$.

**(B) Yes.** The graph is properly nested (series–parallel): one parallel block followed by a sequence. So parbegin–parend is enough and no semaphores are needed:

```pascal
begin
  parbegin
    read n;                   { S1 }
    i := 1                    { S2 }
  parend;
  if i > n then goto next;    { S3 }
  a(i) := i + 1;              { S4 }
  i := i + 1;                 { S5 }
  next: write a(i)            { S6 }
end
```

**Answer: (A) $S_1 \parallel S_2$, both before $S_3$, then $S_3 \to S_4 \to S_5 \to S_6$; (B) Yes — it is series–parallel, so parbegin–parend alone suffices.**

go_v3_5.24.9.e:
With all semaphores initially 0, a `P(x)` can complete only after the matching `V(x)`. So each semaphore gives a precedence edge from the statement that is followed by `V(x)` to the statement that is preceded by `P(x)`:

| Semaphore | `V` after | `P` before | Edge |
|---|---|---|---|
| a | $S_1$ | $S_2$ | $S_1 \to S_2$ |
| b | $S_1$ | $S_3$ | $S_1 \to S_3$ |
| c | $S_2$ | $S_4$ | $S_2 \to S_4$ |
| d | $S_2$ | $S_5$ | $S_2 \to S_5$ |
| e | $S_4$ | $S_7$ | $S_4 \to S_7$ |
| f | $S_5$ | $S_7$ | $S_5 \to S_7$ |
| g | $S_3$ | $S_6$ | $S_3 \to S_6$ |
| h | $S_3$ | $S_8$ | $S_3 \to S_8$ |
| i | $S_6$ | $S_8$ | $S_6 \to S_8$ |
| j | $S_8$ | $S_9$ | $S_8 \to S_9$ |
| k | $S_7$ | $S_9$ | $S_7 \to S_9$ |

Precedence graph (arrows point downward):

```text
            S1
          /    \
        S2      S3
       /  \    /  \

        S7       S8
```

A certain processor provides a 'test and set' instruction that is used as follows:

```text
TSET register, flag
```

This instruction atomically copies flag to register and sets flag to $1$. Give pseudo-code for implementing the entry and exit code to a critical region using this instruction.
go_v3_5.24.16.e:
Use a shared lock variable `flag` with $0$ = region free and $1$ = region occupied, initialised to $0$.

- **Entry:** execute `TSET R, flag` repeatedly. Because the instruction is atomic, the old value of `flag` is copied to `R` and `flag` becomes 1 in one indivisible step. If `R = 0`, the region was free and this process is the one that set it to 1, so it enters. If `R = 1`, another process is inside, so it tries again (busy waiting).
- **Exit:** store `flag := 0`, releasing the region.

```text
; shared: flag = 0 initially
entry:  TSET  R, flag      ; R <- flag, flag <- 1   (atomic)
        CMP   R, #0
        JNZ   entry        ; R = 1: region busy, keep trying
        ; ----- critical region -----
exit:   MOV   flag, #0     ; release the region
        ; ----- remainder section -----
```

The same in high-level form:

```text
repeat
    TSET R, flag
until R = 0;
    <critical region>
flag := 0;
```

**Mutual exclusion:** when several processes execute `TSET` at the same time, the hardware serialises them; only the first one reads $0$ and all the others read $1$ until the exit code stores $0$. **Progress** also holds (if the region is free, some contender's `TSET` returns 0). **Bounded waiting** is not guaranteed, though: a process can keep losing the race. Waiting processes spin, so this is a spin lock.

**Answer: Entry: `repeat TSET R, flag until R = 0`; Exit: `flag := 0` (with `flag` initially 0).**

**Key idea: the "lost wake-up" race.** Testing `count` and going to sleep are two separate steps. A `Wakeup` sent to a process that has *decided* to sleep but has not slept yet is simply lost, because wakeups are not remembered.

**Interleaving (count = 0 initially):**

| Step | Process | Action | count |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Consumer | tests `count = 0` → true, decides to sleep … **preempted before `sleep`** | 0 |
| 2 | Producer | produces an item; `count = 1`? No, so it does not sleep | 0 |
| 3 | Producer | places the item in the buffer; `count = 1` | 1 |
| 4 | Producer | `Wakeup(Consumer)`: the Consumer is not asleep yet, so the wakeup is **lost** | 1 |
| 5 | Producer | next iteration: produces an item; tests `count = 1` → true → **sleeps** | 1 |
| 6 | Consumer | resumes and executes its pending `sleep` → **sleeps** | 1 |

The Producer now waits for the Consumer to empty the buffer. The Consumer waits for a wakeup that can never come, because the only process that could send it is itself asleep. Both processes sleep forever, which is a deadlock.

Making each individual test or assignment atomic does not help. The whole "test-then-sleep" sequence would have to be atomic, for example by using semaphores, whose counts remember pending wakeups.

At any moment the token is in exactly one place: in $S$, in $Q$, or with the one thread that is between its $P$ and its $V$. In particular, $S + Q \le 1$.

1. At the start $S = 1$ and $Q = 0$, so only the producer can pass `P(S)`. It sets `x`, then `V(Q)` makes $Q = 1$.
2. The producer loops to `P(S)` and blocks because $S = 0$. The consumer passes `P(Q)`, consumes `x`, and `V(S)` makes $S = 1$.
3. The consumer loops to `P(Q)` and blocks, the producer continues, and the cycle repeats.

Consequences:
- **(A) is false:** exactly one thread can always proceed, so there is no deadlock.
- **(B) is false:** the threads strictly alternate, so each gets its turn after one step of the other and neither starves.
- **(C) is false:** the producer cannot overwrite `x` until the consumer has consumed it and done `V(S)`, so no item is lost.
- **(D) is true:** every value in `x` is consumed before the producer can produce the next one.

**Answer: (D)**

go_v3_5.25.1.q:
A number of processes could be in a deadlock state if none of them can execute due to non-availability of sufficient resources. Let $P_i, 0 \le i \le 4$ represent five processes and let there be four resources types $r_j, 0 \le j \le 3$. Suppose the following data structures have been used.

**Available:** A vector of length $4$ such that if Available $[i] = k$, there are k instances of resource type $r_j$ available in the system.

**Allocation.** A $5 \times 4$ matrix defining the number of each type currently allocated to each process. If Allocation $[i, j] = k$ then process $p_i$ is currently allocated $k$ instances of resource type $r_j$.

**Max.** A $5 \times 4$ matrix indicating the maximum resource need of each process. If $Max[i, j] = k$ then process $p_i$, may need a maximum of $k$ instances of resource type $r_j$ in order to complete the task.

Assume that system allocated resources only when it does not lead into an unsafe state such that resource requirements in future never cause a deadlock state. Now consider the following snapshot of the system.

**Allocation**

| | $r_0$ | $r_1$ | $r_2$ | $r_3$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $p_0$ | 0 | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| $p_1$ | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| $p_2$ | 1 | 3 | 5 | 4 |
| $p_3$ | 0 | 6 | 3 | 2 |
| $p_4$ | 0 | 0 | 1 | 4 |

**Max**

| | $r_0$ | $r_1$ | $r_2$ | $r_3$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $p_0$ | 0 | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| $p_1$ | 1 | 7 | 5 | 0 |
| $p_2$ | 2 | 3 | 5 | 6 |
| $p_3$ | 0 | 6 | 5 | 2 |
| $p_4$ | 0 | 6 | 5 | 6 |

**Available**

| $r_0$ | $r_1$ | $r_2$ | $r_3$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5 | 2 | 0 |

Is the system currently in a safe state? If yes, explain why.
go_v3_5.25.1.e:
**Key idea (Banker's safety algorithm):** the state is safe if the processes can be ordered so that each one can get its *remaining* need from what is available now plus what the earlier processes release when they finish.

**Need = Max − Allocation**

| | $r_0$ | $r_1$ | $r_2$ | $r_3$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $p_0$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| $p_1$ | 0 | 7 | 5 | 0 |
| $p_2$ | 1 | 0 | 0 | 2 |
| $p_3$ | 0 | 0 | 2 | 0 |
| $p_4$ | 0 | 6 | 4 | 2 |

**Safety check**, starting with Work = Available = (1, 5, 2, 0):

| Step | Process | Need ≤ Work? | Work after it finishes (+ its Allocation) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $p_0$ | (0,0,0,0) ≤ (1,5,2,0) ✓ | (1, 5, 3, 2) |
| 2 | $p_2$ | (1,0,0,2) ≤ (1,5,3,2) ✓ | (2, 8, 8, 6) |
| 3 | $p_3$ | (0,0,2,0) ≤ (2,8,8,6) ✓ | (2, 14, 11, 8) |
| 4 | $p_1$ | (0,7,5,0) ≤ (2,14,11,8) ✓ | (3, 14, 11, 8) |
| 5 | $p_4$ | (0,6,4,2) ≤ (3,14,11,8) ✓ | (3, 14, 12, 12) |

All five processes can finish, so ⟨$p_0, p_2, p_3, p_1, p_4$⟩ is a safe sequence. Others exist too, for example ⟨$p_0, p_2, p_3, p_4, p_1$⟩. As a check, the final Work (3, 14, 12, 12) equals the total number of instances of each resource type.

**Why this means the state is safe:** even if every process immediately asks for its full remaining need, the OS can satisfy them one at a time in this order. Each process finishes and returns its resources, so the current state cannot lead to deadlock.

**Answer: Yes, the system is in a safe state (safe sequence ⟨p0, p2, p3, p1, p4⟩).**

go_v3_5.25.2.q:
i. A system of four concurrent processes, $P, Q, R$ and $S$, use shared resources $A, B$ and $C$. The sequences in which processes, $P, Q, R$ and $S$ request and release resources are as follows:

| Process P: | Process Q: | Process R: | Process S: |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. P requests A | 1. Q requests C | 1. R requests B | 1. S requests A |
| 2. P requests B | 2. Q requests A | 2. R requests C | 2. S requests C |
| 3. P releases A | 3. Q releases C | 3. R releases B | 3. S releases A |
| 4. P releases B | 4. P releases A | 4. R releases C | 4. S releases C |

If a resource is free, it is granted to a requesting process immediately. There is no preemption of granted resources. A resource is taken back from a process only when the process explicitly releases it.

Can the system of four processes get into a deadlock? If yes, give a sequence (ordering) of operations (for requesting and releasing resources) of these processes which leads to a deadlock.

ii. Will the processes always get into a deadlock? If your answer is no, give a sequence of these operations which leads to completion of all processes.

iii. What strategies can be used to prevent deadlocks in a system of concurrent processes using shared resources if preemption of granted resources is not allowed?
go_v3_5.25.2.e:
**Key idea:** with no preemption and hold-and-wait allowed, a deadlock needs a **cycle** of processes, each holding one resource and requesting one held by the next. The hold/request pairs are: P holds A and wants B; Q holds C and wants A; R holds B and wants C; S holds A and wants C.

**(i) Yes, a deadlock is possible.** Example ordering:

| # | Operation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | P requests A | granted |
| 2 | Q requests C | granted |
| 3 | R requests B | granted |
| 4 | P requests B | blocked (R holds B) |
| 5 | Q requests A | blocked (P holds A) |
| 6 | R requests C | blocked (Q holds C) |

This gives the wait-for cycle P → R → Q → P: P waits for B (held by R), R waits for C (held by Q), and Q waits for A (held by P). None of them can release anything, so P, Q and R are deadlocked. S will also block forever when it requests A.

A smaller deadlock also exists: S requests A, Q requests C, S requests C (blocked by Q), Q requests A (blocked by S). This gives the cycle S ⇄ Q.

**(ii) No, deadlock is not inevitable.** For example, run the processes one after another:
P: req A, req B, rel A, rel B → Q: req C, req A, rel C, rel A → R: req B, req C, rel B, rel C → S: req A, req C, rel A, rel C.
Every request finds its resource free, so all four processes complete.

**(iii) Prevention without preemption.** Since preemption is ruled out, make one of the other necessary conditions impossible:
1. **Break hold-and-wait:** a process requests all the resources it needs at once and gets them only if all are free. Alternatively, it must release everything it holds before requesting more.
2. **Break circular wait:** impose a total order on resource types (e.g. A < B < C) and require every process to request resources in increasing order. Here only Q breaks the order (C before A). If Q requests A first and then C, no cycle can form.
3. **Weaken mutual exclusion** where possible: make resources sharable (e.g. read-only data) or spool them, so that no process waits for exclusive access.

Deadlock *avoidance* is another option when maximum needs are known in advance: a request is granted only if the state stays safe, as in the Banker's algorithm.

**Answer: (i) Yes (e.g. the P–R–Q cycle above); (ii) No (running them one after another completes all four); (iii) eliminate hold-and-wait or circular wait (resource ordering), or relax mutual exclusion.**

go_v3_5.25.8.q:
An operating system handles requests to resources as follows.

A process (which asks for some resources, uses them for some time and then exits the system) is assigned a unique timestamp are when it starts. The timestamps are monotonically increasing with time. Let us denote the timestamp of a process $P$ by $TS(P)$.

When a process $P$ requests for a resource the $OS$ does the following:

i. If no other process is currently holding the resource, the $OS$ awards the resource to $P$.

ii. If some process $Q$ with $TS(Q) < TS(P)$ is holding the resource, the $OS$ makes $P$ wait for the resources.

iii. If some process $Q$ with $TS(Q) > TS(P)$ is holding the resource, the $OS$ restarts $Q$ and awards the resources to $P$. (Restarting means taking back the resources held by a process, killing it and starting it again with the same timestamp)

When a process releases a resource, the process with the smallest timestamp (if any) amongst those waiting for the resource is awarded the resource.

A. Can a deadlock over arise? If yes, show how. If not prove it.

B. Can a process P ever starve? If yes, show how. If not prove it.
go_v3_5.25.8.e:
**Key idea:** this is the *wound–wait* scheme. An older process (smaller timestamp) preempts, or "wounds", a younger holder, while a younger process waits for an older holder.

**A. Deadlock cannot arise.**

*Claim:* whenever $P$ waits for a resource held by $Q$, $TS(P) > TS(Q)$, i.e. a younger process waits for an older one.
- A process waits only under rule (ii), where the holder is older.
- Under rule (iii) the older requester never waits; instead the younger holder is restarted and loses its resources.
- On a release, the resource goes to the **oldest** waiter $W$. All the other waiters for that resource are younger than $W$, so they are still younger processes waiting for an older one. Similarly, after rule (iii) gives the resource to $P$, the remaining waiters were younger than the old holder $Q$, and hence also younger than $P$.

So every edge $P \to Q$ in the wait-for graph has $TS(P) > TS(Q)$. Timestamps strictly decrease along any path, so a path can never return to where it started and the graph has no cycle. A deadlock needs a cycle of waiting processes, so no deadlock is possible.

**B. No process starves.**

- A restarted process keeps its **original** timestamp, so restarts never make it "younger". New processes always get larger timestamps.
- Consider the oldest process $O$ currently in the system. It never waits, because any holder is younger and rule (iii) applies. It is never restarted, because only a strictly older requester could restart it. So $O$ runs to completion in finite time and leaves.
- Now take any process $P$. Only finitely many processes are older than $P$ (those that started before it), and no new process can ever be older than $P$. By the previous point these older processes finish one by one, each becoming the oldest in turn. Each of them can restart $P$ only finitely often during its finite lifetime. Once they have all left, $P$ is the oldest process and runs to completion.

So every process eventually finishes, and no process starves.

**Answer: A: No deadlock (waits only go from younger to older, so there is no cycle). B: No starvation (timestamps are kept, so every process eventually becomes the oldest and completes).**

go_v3_5.25.11.q:
Two concurrent processes $P1$ and $P2$ want to use resources $R1$ and $R2$ in a mutually exclusive manner. Initially, $R1$ and $R2$ are free. The programs executed by the two processes are given below.

| **Program for P1:** | **Program for P2:** |
|---|---|
| S1: While ($R1$ is busy) do no-op; | Q1: While ($R1$ is busy) do no-op; |
| S2: Set $R1 \leftarrow$ busy; | Q2: Set $R1 \leftarrow$ busy; |
| S3: While ($R2$ is busy) do no-op; | Q3: While ($R2$ is busy) do no-op; |
| S4: Set $R2 \leftarrow$ busy; | Q4: Set $R2 \leftarrow$ busy; |
| S5: Use $R1$ and $R2$; | Q5: Use $R1$ and $R2$; |
| S6: Set $R1 \leftarrow$ free; | Q6: Set $R2 \leftarrow$ free; |
| S7: Set $R2 \leftarrow$ free; | Q7: Set $R1 \leftarrow$ free; |

A. Is mutual exclusion guaranteed for $R1$ and $R2$? If not show a possible interleaving of the statements of $P1$ and $P2$ such mutual exclusion is violated (i.e., both $P1$ and $P2$ use $R1$ and $R2$ at the same time).

B. Can deadlock occur in the above program? If yes, show a possible interleaving of the statements of $P1$ and $P2$ leading to deadlock.

C. Exchange the statements $Q1$ and $Q3$ and statements $Q2$ and $Q4$. Is mutual exclusion guaranteed now? Can deadlock occur?
go_v3_5.25.11.e:
**Key idea:** "While (busy) do no-op" followed by "Set busy" is a test followed by a separate set, not one atomic step, so two processes can both see a resource as free. Deadlock is a separate question: it needs the two processes to take the resources in opposite orders.

**A. Mutual exclusion is not guaranteed.** One interleaving, with both resources free at the start:

S1 (R1 free) → Q1 (R1 still free) → S2 (R1 ← busy) → Q2 (R1 ← busy) → S3 (R2 free) → Q3 (R2 still free) → S4 → Q4 → **S5 and Q5**. Both processes now use R1 and R2 at the same time.

**B. Deadlock cannot occur.** Both processes acquire the resources in the **same order** (R1, then R2). Each program is a finite sequence that frees both resources after using them.
- A process spinning at S1 or Q1 is waiting for R1. R1 is busy only because the other process has passed S2 or Q2, and that process needs only R2 from then on.
- R2 can be busy only if some process has passed S4 or Q4. Such a process needs nothing more: it uses the resources and frees them.

So the situation "each holds one resource and waits for the other" never arises, and every spinning process is eventually released. Checking all interleavings confirms that no stuck state is reachable.

**C. After the swap, P2 becomes:**
Q3: While (R2 busy) no-op; Q4: Set R2 ← busy; Q1: While (R1 busy) no-op; Q2: Set R1 ← busy; Q5; Q6; Q7.

*Mutual exclusion is now guaranteed.* Suppose both reach the "use" step. P1 must have found R2 free at S3, which comes after its S2 (R1 ← busy). P2 must have found R1 free at Q1, which comes after its Q4 (R2 ← busy). Neither resource is freed before its holder finishes using it. So R1 being free at Q1 means Q1 happened before S2, and R2 being free at S3 means S3 happened before Q4. Together with program order this gives S2 < S3 < Q4 < Q1 < S2, which is impossible. So at most one process can be using the resources.

*Deadlock can occur*, because the processes now take the resources in opposite orders:
S1 → S2 (P1 holds R1) → Q3 → Q4 (P2 holds R2) → S3 (P1 spins waiting for R2) → Q1 (P2 spins waiting for R1). Each holds one resource and busy-waits for the other forever.

**Answer: A: No (interleaving above); B: No deadlock; C: mutual exclusion is guaranteed, but deadlock is possible.**

go_v3_5.25.23.q:
A system shares $9$ tape drives. The current allocation and maximum requirement of tape drives for that processes are shown below:

| Process | Current Allocation | Maximum Requirement |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| P1 | 3 | 7 |
| P2 | 1 | 6 |
| P3 | 3 | 5 |

Which of the following best describes current state of the system?
go_v3_5.25.23.e:
**Key idea:** run the Banker's safety check. If there is an order in which every process can get its remaining need and finish, the state is safe, and a safe state is never deadlocked.

Available drives $= 9 - (3+1+3) = 2$.

| Process | Allocation | Max | Need = Max − Alloc |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| P1 | 3 | 7 | 4 |
| P2 | 1 | 6 | 5 |
| P3 | 3 | 5 | 2 |

- Available $= 2 \ge$ Need(P3) $= 2$. P3 gets its 2 drives, finishes and releases all 5 it holds, so Available $= 2 + 3 = 5$.
- Need(P2) $= 5 \le 5$. P2 finishes, so Available $= 5 + 1 = 6$.
- Need(P1) $= 4 \le 6$. P1 finishes, so Available $= 9$.

The safe sequence is $\langle P3, P2, P1\rangle$ ($\langle P3, P1, P2\rangle$ also works). The state is **safe**, so it is also **not deadlocked**.

- A is self-contradictory, because a deadlocked state is always unsafe.
- C and D are wrong because a safe sequence exists.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v3_5.25.26.q:
Two shared resources $R_1$ and $R_2$ are used by processes $P_1$ and $P_2$. Each process has a certain priority for accessing each resource. Let $T_{ij}$ denote the priority of $P_i$ for accessing $R_j$. A process $P_i$ can snatch a resource $R_k$ from process $P_j$ if $T_{ik}$ is greater than $T_{jk}$.

Given the following :

I. $T_{11} > T_{21}$

II. $T_{12} > T_{22}$

III. $T_{11} < T_{21}$

IV. $T_{12} < T_{22}$

Which of the following conditions ensures that $P_1$ and $P_2$ can never deadlock?
go_v3_5.25.26.e:
**Key idea:** for $P_1$ and $P_2$ to deadlock, each must hold one resource and wait for the other, with **neither** able to snatch what it wants. Snatching (preemption) breaks the cycle if at least one of them can take the resource it is waiting for.

**(I) and (II):** $T_{11} > T_{21}$ and $T_{12} > T_{22}$, so $P_1$ has the higher priority on **both** resources. Whatever $P_1$ needs, it can snatch from $P_2$, so $P_1$ never waits. A wait-for cycle would need $P_1$ to wait, so no deadlock is possible: $P_1$ finishes and releases its resources, and then $P_2$ proceeds. ✔

**(I) and (IV):** $P_1$ dominates $R_1$ and $P_2$ dominates $R_2$. Deadlock is possible: $P_1$ holds $R_1$ and requests $R_2$, which $P_2$ holds, and it cannot snatch it because $T_{12} < T_{22}$. Meanwhile $P_2$ holds $R_2$ and requests $R_1$, which $P_1$ holds, and it cannot snatch it because $T_{21} < T_{11}$. Both wait forever.

**(II) and (III):** the mirror case. $P_1$ holds $R_2$ (where it is stronger) and wants $R_1$, while $P_2$ holds $R_1$ and wants $R_2$. Neither can snatch, so they deadlock.

So of the pairs offered, only (I) and (II) rule out deadlock. By symmetry, (III) and (IV) would also work, but that pair is not an option.

**Answer: (C)**

go_v3_5.25.27.q: An operating system implements a policy that requires a process to release all resources before making a request for another resource. Select the TRUE statement from the following:
o: Both starvation and deadlock can occur
Starvation can occur but deadlock cannot occur
Starvation cannot occur but deadlock can occur
Neither starvation nor deadlock can occur
go_v3_5.25.27.e:
**Key idea:** the policy removes the **hold-and-wait** condition: a process never holds some resources while waiting for others.

**Deadlock cannot occur.** A deadlock needs all four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait. Under this policy a waiting process holds nothing, so it cannot be part of a cycle in which each process holds a resource needed by the next. Hence there is no deadlock.

**Starvation can occur.** A process that needs several resources together must give up everything before each new request and then ask for them again, typically all together. If some of those resources are popular, another process may be holding at least one of them every time it asks, so it can wait indefinitely while others keep being served. Nothing in the policy guarantees that every request is eventually granted, and it also lowers resource utilisation.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v3_5.28.11.e:
**Key idea:** this is the classical (Hoare-style) monitor built from semaphores. A process doing `x.wait` must give up the monitor and then **block on `x_sem`**. A process doing `x.signal` must **wake one process blocked on `x_sem`** and then suspend itself on `next` (signal-and-wait).

- **E1 (in `x.wait`) = `P(x_sem)`.** After incrementing `x_count`, the waiter hands the monitor to someone else: `V(next)` if a signaller is suspended, otherwise `V(mutex)`. It must then sleep until it is signalled. `x_sem` starts at 0, so `P(x_sem)` blocks it. When woken, it decrements `x_count` and continues inside the monitor.
- **E2 (in `x.signal`) = `V(x_sem)`.** If some process is waiting (`x_count > 0`), the signaller records itself in `next_count`, wakes one waiter with `V(x_sem)`, and blocks itself with `P(next)`, so the woken process has the monitor to itself. When that process leaves or waits again, it sees `next_count > 0` and does `V(next)`, which resumes the signaller.

Why the others fail:
- **(A)** Using `V(next)` as E2 would wake some other suspended signaller instead of the process waiting on $x$, so that waiter is never woken.
- **(C)** Using `P(next)` as E1 makes the waiter block on the wrong semaphore.
- **(B)** Here a waiting process would signal `next` instead of going to sleep.

**Answer: (D)**

go_v3_5.31.5.e:
All threads of a process execute in the **same address space**. The code segment, the data segment (global and static variables) and the heap are all part of that address space and are therefore shared: a global written by one thread is seen by the others, and memory obtained with `malloc` by one thread can be used and freed by another.

Only the execution context is private to each thread: thread id, program counter, registers and the **stack** (local variables, return addresses).

So threads share both the heap and the global variables — which is exactly why accesses to them need synchronisation.

**Answer: (D)**

go_v3_5.31.6.q:
Which of the following is/are shared by all the threads in a process?

I. Program counter

II. Stack

III. Address space

IV. Registers
go_v3_5.31.6.e:
A thread is an independent flow of control *inside* a process, so each thread needs its own execution state:
- **Program counter** — each thread is at its own point in the code (private);
- **Registers** — saved and restored per thread on a thread switch (private);
- **Stack** — each thread has its own call frames and local variables (private).

What all threads share is what belongs to the process: the **address space** (code, globals, heap), open files, signal handlers, etc.

So only (III) is shared.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v3_5.31.10.q: Which one of the following is NOT shared by the threads of the same process ?
go_v3_5.31.10.e:
Threads of a process share all **process-level resources**: the address space (code, global data, heap), the open files (file-descriptor table), signal dispositions, and IPC objects such as message queues owned by the process.

What each thread must have privately is its own **execution context**: thread id, program counter, register set and its own **stack**, which holds that thread's chain of function calls, local variables and return addresses. If two threads used one stack, their call frames would overwrite each other.

(Because all threads live in one address space, a thread *can* reach another thread's stack through a pointer, but each thread is given its own separate stack.)

**Answer: (A)**

go_v3_5.33.4.q: Indicate all the false statements from the statements given below:
o: The amount of virtual memory available is limited by the availability of the secondary memory
Any implementation of a critical section requires the use of an indivisible machine-instruction, such as test-and-set.
The use of monitors ensure that no dead-locks will be caused.
The LRU page-replacement policy may cause thrashing for some type of programs.
The best fit techniques for memory allocation ensures that memory will never be fragmented.
go_v3_5.33.4.e:
Check each statement on its own.

- **A: True.** Pages of a process that are not in RAM must be kept on the backing store (swap space). The virtual memory that can actually be provided is therefore bounded by the secondary storage available for it, as well as by the address size.
- **B: False.** Mutual exclusion can be achieved purely in software using ordinary atomic loads and stores, for example with Dekker's algorithm, Peterson's algorithm or Lamport's bakery algorithm. Test-and-set and similar instructions make it easier, but they are not required.
- **C: False.** A monitor only guarantees that one process at a time is active inside it, which is mutual exclusion. Deadlock is still possible. Examples:
  - nested monitor calls, where a process inside $M_1$ calls $M_2$ while another process inside $M_2$ calls $M_1$;
  - processes waiting on condition variables that nobody will ever signal.
- **D: True.** Thrashing happens whenever a process's working set does not fit in its frames, whatever the replacement policy. For example, cycling through $n+1$ pages with $n$ frames makes LRU fault on every single reference.
- **E: False.** Best fit leaves the smallest possible leftover holes. These are usually too small to use, so external fragmentation still happens (it is in fact typical of best fit).

The false statements are B, C and E.

**Answer: B, C, E**

go_v3_5.33.5.q: Which one of the following statements is true?
o: Macro definitions cannot appear within other macro definitions in assembly language programs
Overlaying is used to run a program which is longer than the address space of a computer
Virtual memory can be used to accommodate a program which is longer than the address space of a computer
It is not possible to write interrupt service routines in a high level language
go_v3_5.33.5.e:
**Key idea:** keep physical memory and address space apart.
- Virtual memory lets a program be larger than **physical memory**, but never larger than the **virtual address space**, because every byte of the program needs a virtual address.
- Overlays get around the address limit by loading different parts of the program into the **same** address range at different times.

**Checking each statement**
- **A: False.** Macro processors allow a macro definition inside another macro definition. The inner macro becomes defined when the outer one is called. Nested macro *calls* are allowed too.
- **B: True.** The programmer splits the program into a resident root and overlay segments that are never needed at the same time. These segments are loaded on top of one another in one region, so the whole program can be larger than the addressable memory. Overlays were used this way on 16-bit machines such as the PDP-11, whose address space was 64 KB.
- **C: False.** Virtual memory maps a large virtual address space onto a smaller physical memory. A program larger than the virtual address space cannot even be addressed.
- **D: False.** Interrupt service routines are routinely written in C. This is done either with a compiler's `interrupt` attribute or with a short assembly stub that saves the registers and calls a C handler. Operating-system kernels do this all the time.

**Answer: (B)**
go_v3_5.33.5.note: Disputed: the worked solution below concludes B, but the answer key gives A. This has not had its second check yet, so grading uses the key. The key says A, but macro assemblers allow a macro definition inside another (macro-defining macros), so A is false. B is the only true statement: overlays reuse one address range, while virtual memory is limited by the virtual address space.

go_v3_5.33.21.q: A CPU generates $32$-bit virtual addresses. The page size is $4$ KB. The processor has a translation look-aside buffer (TLB) which can hold a total of $128$ page table entries and is $4$-way set associative. The minimum size of the TLB tag is:
go_v3_5.33.21.e:
**Key idea:** a TLB is a cache keyed by the virtual page number (VPN). In a set-associative TLB, the low-order VPN bits select the set, and the remaining VPN bits must be stored as the tag.

- Page offset $= \log_2(4\text{K}) = 12$ bits, so VPN $= 32 - 12 = 20$ bits.
- Number of sets $= \dfrac{128}{4} = 32 = 2^5$, so the set index is $5$ bits.
- Tag $= 20 - 5 = 15$ bits.

Option D ($20$ bits) would be correct only for a fully associative TLB, which has no index bits.

**Answer: (C)**

go_v3_5.33.26.q: Let the page fault service time be $10$ milliseconds(ms) in a computer with average memory access time being $20$ nanoseconds (ns). If one page fault is generated every $10^6$ memory accesses, what is the effective access time for memory?
go_v3_5.33.26.e:
**Key idea:** the effective access time is the normal access time plus the page-fault cost, weighted by how often faults happen.

- Page-fault rate: $p = 10^{-6}$
- Service time: $10 \text{ ms} = 10^{7}$ ns

$$\text{EAT} = (1-p)\cdot 20 + p\,(10^{7} + 20) = 20 + p \cdot 10^{7} = 20 + 10^{-6}\times 10^{7} = 20 + 10 = 30 \text{ ns}$$

A single fault costs $10^{7}$ ns. Spread over $10^{6}$ accesses, that adds $10$ ns to every access.

**Answer: (B)**

go_v3_5.33.27.q:
A computer uses $46$-bit virtual address, $32$-bit physical address, and a three–level paged page table organization. The page table base register stores the base address of the first-level table $(T1)$, which occupies exactly one page. Each entry of $T1$ stores the base address of a page of the second-level table $(T2)$. Each entry of $T2$ stores the base address of a page of the third-level table $(T3)$. Each entry of $T3$ stores a page table entry $(\text{PTE})$. The $\text{PTE}$ is $32$ bits in size. The processor used in the computer has a $1$ MB $16$ way set associative virtually indexed physically tagged cache. The cache block size is $64$ bytes.

What is the size of a page in KB in this computer?
go_v3_5.33.27.e:
**Key idea:** every table at every level is exactly one page. With 4-byte entries, each level therefore indexes $p-2$ bits of the virtual address, where $2^p$ is the page size.

Let the page size be $2^p$ bytes. An entry is $32$ bits $= 4 = 2^2$ bytes, so one page of a table holds $2^{p-2}$ entries. Each of the three levels then consumes $p-2$ bits of the virtual address, and the page offset takes the remaining $p$ bits:

$$3(p-2) + p = 46 \;\Rightarrow\; 4p = 52 \;\Rightarrow\; p = 13$$

The page size is $2^{13}$ B $= 8$ KB.

**Check:** the virtual address splits as $11 \mid 11 \mid 11 \mid 13 = 46$ bits. T1 has $2^{11}$ entries $\times 4$ B $= 8$ KB, which is exactly one page, as the question requires.

**Why the other sizes fail:**
- $4$ KB ($p = 12$): T3 and T2 index $10$ bits each, which leaves $46 - 32 = 14$ bits for T1. T1 would then be $2^{14} \times 4$ B $= 64$ KB, i.e. 16 pages, not one.
- $16$ KB ($p = 14$): T3 and T2 index $12$ bits each, which leaves only $8$ bits for T1. T1 would be $1$ KB, less than a page.
- $2$ KB is worse than $4$ KB in the same way as the $4$ KB case.

The cache data is not needed here; it is used in the follow-up question on page colouring.

**Answer: (C)**

go_v3_5.33.28.q:
A computer uses $46$-bit virtual address, $32$-bit physical address, and a three–level paged page table organization. The page table base register stores the base address of the first-level table $(T1)$, which occupies exactly one page. Each entry of $T1$ stores the base address of a page of the second-level table $(T2)$. Each entry of $T2$ stores the base address of a page of the third-level table $(T3)$. Each entry of $T3$ stores a page table entry $(\text{PTE})$. The $\text{PTE}$ is $32$ bits in size. The processor used in the computer has a $1$ MB $16$ way set associative virtually indexed physically tagged cache. The cache block size is $64$ bytes.

What is the minimum number of page colours needed to guarantee that no two synonyms map to different sets in the processor cache of this computer?
go_v3_5.33.28.e:
**Key idea:** the cache is virtually indexed, so the set is chosen from virtual-address bits. Synonyms are different virtual addresses that map to the same physical address, and they are guaranteed to agree only in the page-offset bits. Any set-index bits above the page offset come from the virtual page number, so synonyms could fall into different sets. Page colouring fixes those bits: pages may alias only if they have the same "colour". The number of colours needed is $2^{(\text{index bits above the page offset})}$.

**Cache geometry**
- Number of sets $= \dfrac{1\text{ MB}}{16 \times 64\text{ B}} = \dfrac{2^{20}}{2^{10}} = 2^{10}$, so there are $10$ set-index bits.
- The block offset is $6$ bits.
- Set selection therefore uses address bits $0$ to $15$, i.e. $16$ bits.

**Page offset:** from the previous part, pages are $8$ KB, so the page offset is $13$ bits.

**Bits from the VPN:** $16 - 13 = 3$ set-index bits lie above the page offset. That gives $2^3 = 8$ colours.

The same result follows directly: one cache way holds $1\text{ MB}/16 = 64$ KB, and $64\text{ KB} / 8\text{ KB} = 8$ colours.

**Answer: (C)**

go_v3_5.33.41.q: In a virtual memory system, size of the virtual address is $32$-bit, size of the physical address is $30$-bit, page size is $4$ Kbyte and size of each page table entry is $32$-bit. The main memory is byte addressable. Which one of the following is the maximum number of bits that can be used for storing protection and other information in each page table entry?
go_v3_5.33.41.e:
**Key idea:** a page table entry must hold the physical **frame number**. Whatever is left of the entry can be used for valid, protection, dirty and other bits.

- Page size $= 4\text{ KB} = 2^{12}$ bytes, so the page offset is $12$ bits.
- Number of frames $= \dfrac{2^{30}}{2^{12}} = 2^{18}$, so the frame number needs $18$ bits.
- Bits left in a $32$-bit entry $= 32 - 18 = 14$.

The $32$-bit virtual address decides how many entries there are ($2^{20}$). It does not change what each entry has to hold.

**Answer: (D)**

go_v3_5.33.42.q: A paging scheme uses a Translation Look-aside Buffer (TLB). A TLB-access takes $10$ ns and the main memory access takes $50$ ns. What is the effective access time(in ns) if the TLB hit ratio is $90\%$ and there is no page-fault?
go_v3_5.33.42.e:
**Key idea:** the TLB is searched first, on every access.
- On a hit, one memory access fetches the data.
- On a miss, there is one extra memory access to read the page-table entry (single-level page table), and then the data access.

| Case | Probability | Time (ns) |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| TLB hit | $0.9$ | $10 + 50 = 60$ |
| TLB miss | $0.1$ | $10 + 50 + 50 = 110$ |

$$\text{EAT} = 0.9 \times 60 + 0.1 \times 110 = 54 + 11 = 65 \text{ ns}$$

Equivalently, $\text{EAT} = 10 + 50 + 0.1 \times 50 = 65$ ns.

Two options come from incomplete sums:
- A ($54$) keeps only the hit term $0.9 \times 60$.
- B ($60$) is the time of a hit alone.

**Answer: (C)**

go_v3_5.33.43.q:
Match the following flag bits used in the context of virtual memory management on the left side with the different purposes on the right side of the table below.

| Name of the bit | Purpose |
|---|---|
| I. Dirty | a. Page initialization |
| II. R/W | b. Write-back policy |
| III. Reference | c. Page protection |
| IV. Valid | d. Page replacement policy |
go_v3_5.33.43.e:
**Key idea:** each page-table flag exists to support one OS decision.

- **I. Dirty (modified) bit → b. Write-back policy.** The bit is set when the page is written. When the page is evicted, only dirty pages are written back to disk; clean pages are simply discarded.
- **II. R/W bit → c. Page protection.** It marks a page as read-only or writable. A write to a read-only page traps to the OS.
- **III. Reference (accessed) bit → d. Page replacement policy.** Hardware sets it on every access, and the OS clears it periodically. Clock (second-chance), NRU and other LRU approximations use it to choose a victim.
- **IV. Valid bit → a. Page initialization.** An invalid entry means the page is not yet loaded or initialised in memory. Touching it causes a page fault, the OS brings in or zero-fills the page, and then marks the entry valid.

The matching is I-b, II-c, III-d, IV-a, which is option D. Options B and C wrongly pair the Reference bit with page initialization.

**Answer: (D)**
